a] [Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal under the proviso to sub-section (2) for approval of the action 
taken by him, the authority concerned shall, without delay, hear such application and pass, ] [within a period of 
three months from the date of receipt of such application] [ Substituted by Act 46_of 1982, Section 17, for " as 
expeditiously as possible" (w.e.f. 21.8.1984).][, such order in relation thereto as it deems fit:]. ][{Provided that 
where any such authority considers it necessary or expedient so to do, it may, for reasons to be recorded in 
writing, extend such period by such further period as it may think fit: Provided further that no proceedings 
before any such authority shall lapse merely on the ground that any period specified in this sub-section had 
expired without such proceedings being completed. | 


10. Of course by enacting sec 33, the legislature wanted to ensure a fair and satisfactory enquiry of the industrial 
dispute undisturbed by any action on the part of the employer or the employee likely to create fresh cause for 
disharmony between them. The legislature visualized that during the pendency of the industrial dispute status quo 
should be maintained and no further element of discord should be introduced between the employer and the 
employee. The objective of the provision of sec 33 is to put a ban on the prerogative of the employer in altering 
the service condition of the employee pending enquiry of the industrial dispute raised by them. The primary 
principle is that if an Industrial Dispute is raised by a group of workmen acting on their own through their union, 
the general conclusion is that the all those who sponsored the dispute are concerned in it. However the very 
factum of raising an Industrial Dispute and pendency of such a dispute in a court of law by an individual employee 
or a group of employees by itself does not lead to the inference that such an individual who alleges retrenchment 
from services was a workman in continuous service under the employer, unless proved by concrete evidence. 
Indeed, Sec 33A stands to the rescue of a workman who alleges alteration or cessation of service by the employer 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 85 


during the pendency of an Industrial Dispute. A regular workman / employee or a casual employee on a 
continuing basis under an employer who files a complaint u/s 33A certainly stands on a different footing than the 
one who claims continuity of service as a casual labourer and whose claim is not accepted by the employer. 


11. The case on hand portrays the scenario the employer disowns and denies the complainant as its regular daily 
wager. The alleged retrenchment of service dated 25.09.2014 averred by the complainant is not accepted or 
recognized by the Oppose Party in the given case. The definite stand of the opposite party is that the complainant 
had been engaged very occasionally and intermittently on need basis to attend menial works like sweeping, 
cleaning etc. without touching the routine works in the office. The complainant per contra very particularly 
pleaded that apart from cleaning in and around the bank office, he was entrusted with the task of assisting 
customers in making challans for cash / cheque, deposits taking and keeping cash in double lock, writing registers, 
collecting cash from other banks from the cheques drawn on them, printing passbooks, deposit receipts, writing 
loan papers, making deposit mobilization, bundling payment slips and day book and such so many tasks. However 
according to the opposite party all the above works are the routine tasks of the regular employees and not of such 
casual workers engaged for attending menial jobs. Thus the factual pleadings of the complainant indicate that his 
engagement in the opposite party bank was not to attend menial labour alone but higher tasks as well, as 
mentioned above. It is while attending such highly responsible tasks in his so called status as MCS / Office 
assistant (multipurpose) / sub-staff at the Mittemari branch of the opposite party continuously since 08.12.2008 
that the opposite party has terminated / retrenched his services on 25.09.2014. This factum also the opposite party 
has emphatically opposed and disputed. According to the opposite party, no such retrenchment or termination has 
ever occurred nor was there any occasion for that as the bank had not engaged the complainant in such a position 
at all in work continuously. In this factual background it is the primary duty of the complainant to substantiate that 
his very entry in the bank was on 08.10.2008 and he continued to perform services in the opposite party bank 
without any break till 25.09.2014. The complainant is equally obliged to prove that he was disengaged from a 
continuous service on 25.09.2014. Inability to offer menial job on a particular date when there was no requirement 
to engage a casual labourer to attend such work pleaded by the opposite party does oblige the complainant to 
substantiate his specific case by adducing reliable and concrete material evidence establishing all the aspects 
pleaded by him in the complaint. The mere pleading raised by him regarding the prevalence / pendency of an 
Industrial Dispute and the so called termination or retrenchment of services on 25.09.2014 without bringing home 
any iota of evidence substantiating the above plea does not bind this Tribunal to accept the case set forth by him as 
gospel truth and to draw a finding against the opposite party. 


12. It is the settled position of law that u/s 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, the complainant carries the initial 
burden / onus to prove that the employer contravened sec 33 of the Act and such contravention occurred during 
the pendency of a dispute, by presenting the facts supported by evidence. Once the complainant discharges his 
initial burden to establish that he is an employee in continuous service within the parameters of sec 33 of the Act 
and such contravention occurred as pleaded and proved, the employer must then justify their actions especially 
concerning alleged dismissal / retrenchment / termination, often leading to the tribunal deciding if the action was 
fair and just like any other Industrial Dispute. 


13. Here in the given case, the one and only aspect accepted and admitted by the opposite party is the pendency 
of CR 22/2013 raised by the Daily Workers Union. That by itself does not discharge the onus of proof cast on the 
complainant to prima facie establish its case. The alleged contravention of service conditions or an illegal 
cessation of the service of an employee by the employer is not an aspect to be simply inferred by the Tribunal out 
of nothing but to be very precisely, meticulously and scrupulously proved and established by the aggrieved 
complainant. 


14. Sec 33A is designed to provide an instant remedy to a workman aggrieved by the contravention of sec 33 by 
filing a complaint before adjudicatory authorities or conciliatory authorities. It is trite that where such a complaint 
is made to an adjudicatory authority viz. Labour Court / Tribunal, it will adjudicate upon the dispute as if it is a 
dispute referred to or pending before it, so that the workman is saved of the botheration of moving the 
Government for referring this dispute for adjudication. 


15. The basic question to be considered by this Tribunal in the complaint on hand u/s 33A is whether there has 
been a contravention by the employer of the provisions of sec 33 and in the event it is found that there has been a 
contravention of the provisions, then to embark upon the exercise to adjudicate about the matter so complained of 
in the complaint on its merit. No written order of termination / retrenchment is produced by the complainant to 
justify his pleadings. Of course, he averred in the complaint that the termination issued by the opposite party was 
only oral. If that be so, it should be proved by the complainant that he was in continuous service under the 
opposite party and was subjected for a termination / retrenchment on an oral order by mounting the witness box. 
Going by the proceedings underwent in the given case, it is clear that once the statement of objection is filed by 
the opposite party, the matter was posted for evidence of the complainant and on the repeated request of the 
complainant, evidence / enquiry was postponed by my learned predecessor by not less than 5 occasions. Then at 
the whimsical stand of the complainant it is made out that there is no need to adduce evidence and the matter be 
posted for arguments. In fact, as per law, before giving any relief to the aggrieved employee under the section, the 


86 


THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 24, 2026/MAGHA 4, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


authority viz., this Tribunal has first to determine that the employee was continuously working under the employer 
and the latter had surreptitiously kicked out him from the job without complying with the mandate u/s 33 of the 
Act. Hence a contravention of sec 33 is the foundation for exercise of the power u/s 33A of the Act. As already 
observed and as rightly pointed out by the learned counsel for the opposite party, no reliable proof / evidence is 
brought on record by the complainant to substantiate that there is contravention of provisions of sec 33 of the Act 
from the side of the opposite party. 


16. In the event if the alleged factum of infraction from the provision of sec 33 is established, the matter has to 
be very meticulously adjudicated on merit to examine whether the complainant is entitled to get an order of 
reinstatement. It is trite that even when contravention of sec 33 is established, that does not automatically lead to 
an order for reinstatement. So, at large, the complainant is at the task to prove and establish the primary elements 
viz., his status as a daily wage employee under the opposite party coupled with contravention of the provisions of 
sec 33 by the latter and then his eventual right to get reinstatement to service with equivalent benefits. 
Determination of all these issues by the legal forum could be possible only when reliable evidence is adduced by 
the complainant by offering himself for searching cross examination by the opposite party in a full-fledged trial. It 
is trite that the initial burden lies on the employee to prove that he falls under the definition of a “workman” under 
the Industrial Disputes Act. If the employee presents a strong prima facie case, the management must then provide 
evidence to rebut it. Of course, the evidence to be adduced by the person claiming to be an employee must be 
substantial, often a preponderance of evidence depending on the claim. It is no longer res-integra that the burden 
of proving the employer-employee relationship primarily rest upon the person who asserts its existence. In a 
situation where a person asserts to be an employee of the management which the management denies, the duty 
primarily rests upon the person so asserting to give positive evidence in his favour and discharge his initial burden. 
At the risk of repetition I say, once such a person has given such a positive evidence in his favour, only then the 
burden would shift on the management to give evidence to counter such claims, because it is always possible to 
prove positive facts than a negative. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Workman of Nilgiri Co-Op Mkt Society 
LTD vs. State of Tamil Nadu (AIR 2004 SC 1639) held that it is a well settled principle of law that the person 
who is setting up a plea of existence of relationship of employer and employee, the burden would be upon him. 
Similar view is adopted by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Bank of Baroda vs. Ghemarabhai Harijibhai Rabari 
(2005 (10) SCC 792). The complainant herein kept aloof from trial feeling shy of an intensive quiz in the witness 
box. Probably, the complainant might have been misled, misguided or mal-advised not to mount the witness box 
so as to avoid probable inconvenience of a grilling cross-examination. The net result of such willful avoidance of 
requisite procedure by the complainant either by himself or as instilled upon him is complete failure of the case 
projected by him. 


17. Extensive argument is advanced on behalf of the complainant with the aid of plethora of legal authorities 
canvassing for a favorable order of reinstatement with full back wages, continuity of service with regularization 
and ancillary benefits from 25.09.2014. As could be heard from Learned Counsel for the opposite party, all these 
wider reliefs sought for by the complainant are the main reliefs claimed in the said case CR 22/2013. By 
consciously avoiding to give oral or documentary evidence in this case, what is craved for on behalf of the 
complainant is to grant the above reliefs even without facing a trial. Granting such reliefs in his favour without 
providing / supplementing any sort of evidentiary support would tantamount to prejudging the issue raised in the 
Industrial Dispute case CR 22/2013 in a very shortcut method. 


18. Argument is advanced on behalf of the complainant placing reliance upon the verdicts of the Hon'ble High 
Court of Gujarat in Gujarat State Electricity Corporation LTD vs. Bhimrao Aagete (LPA 177 / 2016 dated 
06.03.2018), Kalavatiben Prabhakar Patil and others vs. Managing Director (C/SCA/3189/2020 dated 
17.01.2022) that while deciding a complaint u/s 33A it is not obligatory for the workman to prove that he had 
worked for 240 days. Those rulings in fact do not indicate that the complainant is not at all under obligation to 
substantiate his basic status under the opposite party to justify the case put forth. 


19. In the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case and the very casual manner in which it is manned by the 
complainant, the plethora of rulings relied upon by him viz., Hindustan Lever LTD vs. Ram Mohan Roy and 
others (AIR 1973 SC 1156) by the Hon'ble Apex Court, Management of Karur Vysya Bank LTD vs. 
Presiding Officer, Industrial Tribunal (2007 II LLJ 459) by the Hon'ble High Court of Madras, M M 
Narayana vs. KSRTC (AIR 2012 (4) KAR R 518) and Karan Kumar vs. Divisional Controller KSRTC (WP 
203333/2019 dated 13.07.2023) by the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka and Deutsche Lufthansa AG vs. Nayan 
Pahwa & others (2025 INSC 998) by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi are not of any help to the complainant as 
in all those cases non-compliance of the provisions by the respective employers are relating to regular employees 
on its payroll. Among the cases noted above, the case of Karur Vysya Bank LTD, MM Narayana and Karan 
Kumar are related to the actions initiated by the respective employers based on misconduct / misdemeanor of the 
respective regular employees in respect of which approval applications were not submitted by the employers. In 
Hindustan Lever’s case also, the complainants were the regular employees of the employer establishment. In 
principle, the fact situations contained in the afore-quoted ruling do not have any application to the case on hand. 


20. Before concluding, it is worthy to pen down that in order to avail the relief provided u/s 33 of the Act, firstly 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 87 


the aggrieved party should prove himself to be a workman within the definition of u/s 2(s) of the Industrial 
Disputes Act and there exists employer-employee relationship between the contesting parties. In conclusion of the 
afore-discussion, I find that the complainant has miserably failed in substantiating his own case. He equally failed 
in refuting / negating the contentions raised by the opposite party that he is only a coolie engaged on need and 
requirement basis without continuity and frequency and hence not governed by any rules and regulations of the 
bank. So also the complainant further failed in successfully controverting the rival contentions of the opposite 
party that there is no employee-employer relationship between himself and the opposite party or that he was not 
engaged by the latter against a sanctioned post. The deliberate refusal, negligence or avoidance to prove and 
establish a genuine and reliable case by tendering requisite evidence has led the complainant to face a total failure 
in the given case and for an eventual dismissal of the complaint. With this view, these points are answered 
accordingly. 


21. Point No. 5:- In view of the findings on point no. 1 10 4, it is held that the complainant is not entitled for any 
reliefs sought for in this complaint. 


22. Point no. 6:- In the result the following award is passed.

ORDER 


1. This is a complaint filed by the complainant u/s 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 raising the 
following contentions: - 


The complainant was appointed by the opposite party in the post of MCS / Office Assistant 
(Multipurpose) / Substaff at their Chelur branch on 09.03.2003 and he worked there for 3 months. Later, on 
09.09.2008 the Branch Manager of Chelur Branch called him to the branch to work by taking application from 
him, interviewing him and on taking documents. Since then he worked continuously in the said branch till the date 
of his termination / retrenchment / discharge / dismissal of his service on 07.04.2013 and asked to work at 
Chilakalanerup branch from 08.04.2013 and he worked in the said branch. Later on 04.09.2014 the Branch 
Manager Mr. Prasad told him that since he filed a case for regularization of service against the Bank through his 
union before this Tribunal, services of the complainant are being terminated and his services are thus terminated. 
Again he was asked to report for work at Chelur Branch by the Branch Manager, Sh. B V Nagaraja, in December 
2015 and the complainant reported for work at the said branch from 20.12.2015. In December 2016 the Branch 
Manager raised an allegation against the complainant that he has stolen a cheque leaf and forged a signature of the 
customer Sh. Reddappa and filled up the cheque and tried to encash the same. On that allegation, the Branch 
Manager Mr. B V Nagaraja, dismissed the service es of the complainant on 12.12.2016. The Branch Manager also 
filed a police complaint against the complainant whereon a criminal case was registered against him. Later based 
on the statement of customer Sh., Reddappa that he had sent the cheque for collection through the complainant, 
the complaint was dismissed. As a part of his job, he used to open the branch by collecting keys from the 
Manager, cleaning the office, aiding the customers and the branch in various ways. In order to avoid the extension 
of status and benefits of permanent workman to him, the Opposite Party directed the Chelur and Chilakalanerup 
branch to debit his wages as coolie charges to the General ledger account without obtaining his signature on the 
debit vouchers. The officials of the branches took his signature on the overleaf of coolie paid debit vouchers along 
with the signatures of the branch officers while paying wages in cash to him. He was the only person doing the 
work of the office attendant / messenger / sweeper / substaff / daily wager / MCS etc on coolie charges. The 
Opposite Party was not marking attendance register for his work, not extended payment register to him, signing 
debit vouchers for his wages by the officers of the bank and receiving amount by them and then paying the 
amounts to him as coolie charges, debiting the wages paid to him to General Ledger Account of the Bank instead 
of salary paid account / Establishment charges, not issuing appointment orders or certificates for the services 
rendered by him in the bank, refusal to pay wages applicable to messengers / housekeeping staff / sub staff / MCS 
to him, not extending the service benefits applicable to permanent workman, taking work from him for years 
together as Coolie by terming his wages as coolie charges practiced by the opposite party are all unfair labour 
practices under the 5" Schedule of the ID Act 1947. The complainant along with other coolie workers of the 
opposite party bank formed a union called Pragathi Grameena Bank Daily Wage Workers Union in 2012 and he 
was active in the Union activities. The Union filed cases before the Central Labour Machinery for getting the 
benefits for the daily wage workers of the Bank. This has caused annoyance to the then management against him. 
CR 22/2013 is pending before this Tribunal in which the Union raised a dispute for regularization of services of 
the workmen including him. He is directly connected with the said dispute raised by the said union. On 
04.09.2014, the Branch Manager asked the complainant not to come for work as his services are terminated 
abruptly without any reason and without issuing any notice to him or paying any retrenchment compensation, 
without following the principles of natural justice. His repeated requests to allow him to do work in the branch 
were not considered by the Branch Manager. The opposite party has not filed any application before the 
appropriate Government seeking permission to retrench him u/s 25 N of the ID Act 1947 nor filed any application 
before this Tribunal for approval of their action in dismissing / discharging / terminating / retrenching his services 
from 12.12.2016. Therefore, the retrenchment of his service is illegal, ab-initio void and he is deemed to be in the 
services of the Bank as per sec 25 N(7) of the ID Act. As per the provision of Sec 33 of the ID Act, the opposite 
party cannot alter or change the conditions of his service applicable to him immediately before the commencement 
of the proceedings of C R 22/2013 to his prejudice, during the pendency of CR 22/2013 before this Tribunal 
without the expressed permission in writing from the tribunal and also shall not discharge / dismiss / terminate / 
retrench him unless he was paid wages for one month and without making an application for approval of the 
action so taken. The opposite party has not complied with any of the provisions of the ID Act 1947 in terminating 
his services. The opposite party was paying him wages @ Rs. 6500/- per month. The opposite party has not paid 
any wages to him since the retrenchment of his services. Since the opposite party has not filed any application 
before the Tribunal seeking approval of their action, he is entitled for payment of full wages drawn by him every 
month till the disposal of this case. He is entitled for wages as per sec 25N (7) of the ID Act. Due to the illegal 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 89 


cessation of service imposed on him by the opposite party, the complainant and his family are suffering 
economically and socially. Hence this complaint for declaring the termination / retrenchment / discharge / 
dismissal of the complainant from 12.12.2016 is not in accordance with the provisions of the ID Act 1947, against 
the principles of natural justice, arbitrary, unilateral, ill motivated and illegal and to direct the opposite party to 
reinstate the complainant with full back wages, continuity of service with regularization, ancillary benefits from 
12.12.2016 and with cost. 


2. The opposite party filed statement of objection resisting the factual averments and relief sought in the 
complaint. It is inter alia contended that the complaint is not maintainable either in law or on facts as there is no 
contravention of the provision of Sec 33 of the ID Act. The opposite party by way of subsequent amalgamations 
is now called as Karnataka Grameena Bank. The service conditions of the employees are governed by Pragathi 
Grameena Bank (Officers and Employees) Service Regulations 2010. The bank used to engage services of the 
workmen occasionally as and when necessitated for doing menial works in the branches when regular office 
attendants remained absent or proceed on leave and for excess work. In order to meet the exigencies of the work, 
the opposite party bank branches used to engage coolies only for few hours for such menial works like cleaning, 
sweeping and watering and were paid coolie charges proportionately depending upon the number of hours they 
worked. The complainant was also engaged similarly as a coolie intermittently and not continuously. Depending 
upon the availability of the person in the locale, the Branch Manager engaged such person on need basis for such 
works. As per the Government of India guidelines for appointment of Regular Attendants, the names should be 
sponsored by the Employment Exchange and such engagement is also subject to the conditions stipulated in 
regard to educational qualification, age etc. While engaging the coolies, no educational qualifications or age were 
looked into and whoever is available would be engaged. The persons so engaged are at liberty to work elsewhere 
after completion of the menial works entrusted to them. They are not governed by any rules and regulation of the 
bank and there is no employee employer relationship as they have not been engaged by the bank against the post. 
There was no requirement at Chilakalanerup branch on 04.09.2014 and he was not engaged for work on that day 
and that cannot be said as refusal of work. The complainant thereafter stopped approaching bank for work. After 
lapse of 3 years, he has filed this complaint alleging violation of the provisions of the sec 33 of the ID Act. The 
daily workers union raised a dispute against the opposite party bank in CR 22/2013 claiming regularization of 
coolies including the complainant. The complaint is not maintainable as there is no refusal of work or termination 
of the services of the complainant. He might have approached the Chelur branch on 20.12.2015 and would have 
been engaged based on requirement. His averment about alleged stealing of a cheque leaf and lodging of police 
complaint and alleged termination on 12.12.2016 are incorrect. On 12.12.2016 he was engaged as there was no 
requirement. Non engagement of the complainant on 12.12.2016 also cannot be characterized as refusal of work or 
termination of his services. The opposite party bank followed the procedures in respect of engagement of and 
payment to the daily wagers. In a case of casual employee, the concept of retrenchment is not attracted if the 
casual is not engaged for want of work on a particular day. Therefore sec 25N of the ID Act referred to in the 
complaint is not attracted. There is no violation of provisions of sec 33 as alleged. The question of filing approval 
application arises only when the termination is for misconduct. In this case there is no termination of complainant 
or any allegation of misconduct against him. Hence the question of filing approval application does not arise. The 
averment that the complainant was paid wages of Rs. 6500/- per month is not correct. He was paid wages by 
calculating the number of days of his engagement. The averment that there is cessation of service by the opposite 
party is not correct. It is the complainant who stopped approaching the bank for work. Hence it is not open for him 
to contend that he and his family members are suffering. The complainant is thus not entitled for any of the reliefs 
prayed for and hence the opposite party sought for rejecting the complaint. 


3. From the above rival pleadings, following points arise for consideration:- 
1. Whether the complaint is legally and factually maintainable? 


2. Whether the Complainant is proved to have been working continuously in the opposite party 
establishment since 20.12.2015? 


3. Whether the complainant is proved to have been discharged / terminated / retrenched / dismissed 
from service on 12.12.2016 as contended by him? 


4. Whether the alleged contravention of the provision of sec 33 of the ID Act is proved by the 
complainant? 


5. Whether the complainant is entitled to get reinstatement to the service with full back wages, 
continuity of service and ancillary benefits from 12.12.2016 as prayed for? 


6. What is the proper Order and Award to be passed in this complaint case? 
4. Either of the parties did not prefer to adduce any evidence in the matter. 
5. Heard the oral and written arguments submitted from both sides. 


6. Points no. 1 to 4:- Since all these points are closely integrated and inter-twined, all these points are 
discussed together. Alleging contravention of the provisions of sec 33 of the ID Act 1947, the complainant filed

the instant complaint u/s 33A of the Act on the factual averment that the opposite party has not filed any 
application before this Tribunal seeking permission for retrenching / terminating / dismissing him on 12.12.2016 
and not filing any application for approval of their said action. The complainant’s case is that he was appointed by 
the opposite party bank at their Chelur branch continuously from 20.12.2015. He claims that since then he has 
worked continuously in the said branch on all working days. It is his further case that to his surprise, without 
giving any prior notice or without assigning any reason, he was asked on 12.12.2016 not to come for work and his 
services are terminated. The complainant inter alia pleaded that he is an active member in a Union under the name 
and style Pragathi Grameena Bank Daily Wage Workers Union formed between himself with other coolie workers 
of the opposite party bank. The said union has raised a dispute for regularization of the service of the complainant 
and other similarly placed coolie before the Central Government Machinery and the same is registered and 
pending before this Tribunal as CR 22/2013. It is the case of the complainant that he is directly connected with the 
said dispute raised by the Union pending before this Tribunal. The disengagement of job on 12.12.2016 according 
to the complainant tantamount to contravention of the provisions of sec 33 of the ID Act as according to him it 
happened when the industrial dispute raised by the union for and on behalf of him and the other coolie workers 
was pending adjudication. According to him the cause for his termination on 12.12.2016 is an alleged stealing and 
forging of a cheque by him, which the opposite party specifically denied. This gave way for filing this complaint 
u/s 33A of the ID Act. 


7. Oral and written arguments are advanced on behalf of the complainant narrating all these events by his 
authorized representative. 


8. The learned counsel for the opposite party per contra put forth his rival submission that the complainant has 
never ever rendered any continuous service in the opposite party bank. Instead the bank was in the practice of 
engaging persons from the locale for attending menial job like sweeping, cleaning and watering when the regular 
employees are absent or proceed on leave and such persons were paid coolie charges for the same. According to 
the opposite party, the complainant was also so casually engaged depending on the requirement of the branch as a 
coolie for doing menial works and such works carried out by him was not regular in nature, but only on need 
basis. To put it differently, according to the opposite party the engagement of the complainant was not continuous 
and it was only intermittent. 


9. Of course, the event of non-engagement for work said to have happened on 12.12.2016 is apparently during 
the pendency of CR 22/2013. However the complainant did not prefer to bring home any proof that he was in 
service in the opposite party bank even on the previous day or anytime there-before in a constant and continuous 
stretch so as to establish the retrenchment / dismissal / discharge / termination alleged in the complaint. Here it is 
contextually profitable to quote Sec 33 of the Act: 


33. [ Conditions of service, etc., to remain unchanged under certain circumstances during pendency of

10. Ofcourse by enacting sec 33, the legislature wanted to ensure a fair and satisfactory enquiry of the industrial 
dispute undisturbed by any action on the part of the employer or the employee likely to create fresh cause for 
disharmony between them. The legislature visualized that during the pendency of the industrial dispute status quo 
should be maintained and no further element of discord should be introduced between the employer and the 
employee. The objective of the provision of sec 33 is to put a ban on the prerogative of the employer in altering 
the service condition of the employee pending enquiry of the industrial dispute raised by them. The primary 
principle is that if an Industrial Dispute is raised by a group of workmen acting on their own through their union, 
the general conclusion is that the all those who sponsored the dispute are concerned in it. However the very 
factum of raising an Industrial Dispute and pendency of such a dispute in a court of law by an individual employee 
or a group of employees by itself does not lead to the inference that such an individual who alleges retrenchment 
from services was a workman in continuous service under the employer, unless proved by concrete evidence. 
Indeed, Sec 33A stands to the rescue of a workman who alleges alteration or cessation of service by the employer 
during the pendency of an Industrial Dispute. A regular workman / employee or a casual employee on a 
continuing basis under an employer who files a complaint u/s 33A certainly stands on a different footing than the 
one who claims continuity of service as a casual labourer and whose claim is not accepted by the employer. 


11. The case on hand portrays the scenario the employer disowns and denies the complainant as its regular daily 
wager. The alleged retrenchment of service dated 12.12.2016 averred by the complainant is not accepted or 
recognized by the Oppose Party in the given case. The definite stand of the opposite party is that the complainant 
had been engaged very occasionally and intermittently on need basis to attend menial works like sweeping, 
cleaning etc. without touching the routine works in the office. The complainant per contra very particularly 
pleaded that apart from cleaning in and around the bank office, he was entrusted with the task of assisting 
customers in making challans for cash / cheque, deposits taking and keeping cash in double lock, writing registers, 
collecting cash from other banks from the cheques drawn on them, printing passbooks, deposit receipts, writing 
loan papers, making deposit mobilization, bundling payment slips and day book and such so many tasks. However 
according to the opposite party all the above works are the routine tasks of the regular employees and not of such 
casual workers engaged for attending menial jobs. Thus the factual pleadings of the complainant indicate that his 
engagement in the opposite party bank was not to attend menial labour alone but higher tasks also, as mentioned 
above. It is while attending such highly responsible tasks in his so called status as MCS / Office assistant 
(multipurpose) / sub-staff at the Chelur branch of the opposite party continuously since 20.12.2015 that the 
opposite party has terminated / retrenched his services on 12.12.2016. This factum also the opposite party has 
emphatically opposed and disputed. According to the opposite party, no such retrenchment or termination has ever 
occurred nor was there any occasion for that as the bank had not engaged the complainant in such a position at all 
in work continuously. In this factual background it is the primary duty of the complainant to substantiate that his 
very entry in the bank was on 09.03.2003 and he continued to perform services in the opposite party bank without 
any break till 04.09.2014 and again got inducted on 20.12.2015 and continued upto 12.12.2016. The complainant 
is obliged to prove that he was disengaged from a continuous service on 12.12.2016. Inability to offer menial job 
on a particular date when there was no requirement to engage a casual labourer to attend such work pleaded by the 
opposite party does oblige the complainant to substantiate his specific case by adducing reliable and concrete 
material evidence establishing all the aspects pleaded by him in the complaint. The mere pleading raised by him 
regarding the prevalence / pendency of an Industrial Dispute and the so called termination or retrenchment of 
services on 12.12.2016 without bringing home any iota of evidence substantiating the above plea does not bind 
this Tribunal to accept the case set forth by him as gospel truth and to draw a finding against the opposite party. 


12. It is the settled position of law that u/s 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, the complainant carries the initial 
burden / onus to prove that the employer contravened sec 33 of the Act and such contravention occurred during 
the pendency of a dispute, by presenting the facts supported by evidence. Once the complainant discharges his 
initial burden to establish that he is an employee in continuous service within the parameters of sec 33 of the Act 
and such contravention occurred as pleaded and proved, the employer must then justify their actions especially 
concerning alleged dismissal / retrenchment / termination, often leading to the tribunal deciding, if the action was 
fair and just like any other Industrial Dispute. 


92 


THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 24, 2026/MAGHA 4, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


13. Here in the given case, the one and only aspect accepted and admitted by the opposite party is the pendency 
of CR 22/2013 raised by the Daily Workers Union. That by itself does not discharge the onus of proof cast on the 
complainant to prima facie establish its case. The alleged contravention of service conditions or an illegal 
cessation of the service of an employee by the employer is not an aspect to be simply inferred by the Tribunal out 
of nothing but to be very precisely, meticulously and scrupulously proved and established by the aggrieved 
complainant. 


14. Sec 33A is designed to provide an instant remedy to a workman aggrieved by the contravention of sec 33 by 
filing a complaint before adjudicatory authorities or conciliatory authorities. It is trite that where such a complaint 
is made to an adjudicatory authority viz. Labour Court / Tribunal, it will adjudicate upon the dispute as if it is a 
dispute referred to or pending before it, so that the workman is saved of the botheration of moving the 
Government for referring this dispute for adjudication. 


15. The basic question to be considered by this Tribunal in the complaint on hand u/s 33A is whether there has 
been a contravention by the employer of the provisions of sec 33 and in the event it is found that there has been a 
contravention of the provisions, then to embark upon the exercise to adjudicate about the matter so complained of 
in the complaint on its merit. No written order of termination / retrenchment is produced by the complainant to 
justify his pleadings. Of course, he averred in the complaint that the termination issued by the opposite party was 
only oral. If that be so, it should be proved by the complainant that he was in continuous service under the 
opposite party and was subjected for a termination / retrenchment on an oral order by mounting the witness box. 
Going by the proceedings underwent in the given case, it is clear that once the statement of objection is filed by 
the opposite party, the matter was posted for evidence of the complainant and on the repeated request of the 
complainant, evidence / enquiry was postponed by my learned predecessor by not less than 5 occasions. Then at 
the whimsical stand of the complainant it is made out that there is no need to adduce evidence and the matter be 
posted for arguments. In fact, as per law, before giving any relief to the aggrieved employee under the section, the 
authority viz., this Tribunal has first to determine that the employee was continuously working under the employer 
and the latter had surreptitiously kicked out him from the job without complying with the mandate u/s 33 of the 
Act. Hence a contravention of sec 33 is the foundation for exercise of the power u/s 33A of the Act. As already 
observed and as rightly pointed out by the learned counsel for the opposite party, no reliable proof / evidence is 
brought on record by the complainant to substantiate that there is contravention of provisions of sec 33 of the Act 
from the side of the opposite party. 


16. In the event if the alleged factum of infraction from the provision of sec 33 is established, the matter has to 
be very meticulously adjudicated on merit to examine whether the complainant is entitled to get an order of 
reinstatement. It is trite that even when contravention of sec 33 is established, that does not automatically lead to 
an order for reinstatement. So, at large, the complainant is at the task to prove and establish the primary elements 
viz., his status as a daily wage employee under the opposite party coupled with contravention of the provisions of 
sec 33 by the latter and then his eventual right to get reinstatement to service with equivalent benefits. 
Determination of all these issues by the legal forum could be possible only when reliable evidence is adduced by 
the complainant by offering himself for searching cross examination by the opposite party in a full-fledged trial. It 
is trite that the initial burden lies on the employee to prove that he falls under the definition of a “workman” under 
the Industrial Disputes Act. If the employee presents a strong prima facie case, the management must then provide 
evidence to rebut it. Of course, the evidence to be adduced by the person claiming to be an employee must be 
substantial, often a preponderance of evidence depending on the claim. It is no longer res-integra that the burden 
of proving the employer-employee relationship primarily rest upon the person who asserts its existence. In a 
situation where a person asserts to be an employee of the management which the management denies, the duty 
primarily rests upon the person so asserting to give positive evidence in his favour and discharge his initial burden. 
At the risk of repetition I say, once such a person has given such a positive evidence in his favour, only then the 
burden would shift on the management to give evidence to counter such claims, because it is always possible to 
prove positive facts than a negative. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Workman of Nilgiri Co-Op Mkt Society 
LTD vs. State of Tamil Nadu (AIR 2004 SC 1639) held that it is a well settled principle of law that the person 
who is setting up a plea of existence of relationship of employer and employee, the burden would be upon him. 
Similar view is adopted by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Bank of Baroda vs. Ghemarabhai Harijibhai Rabari 
(2005 (10) SCC 792). The complainant herein kept aloof from trial feeling shy of an intensive quiz in the witness 
box. Probably, the complainant might have been misled, misguided or mal-advised not to mount the witness box 
so as to avoid probable inconvenience of a grilling cross-examination. The net result of such willful avoidance of 
requisite procedure by the complainant either by himself or as instilled upon him is complete failure of the case 
projected by him. 


17. Extensive argument is advanced on behalf of the complainant with the aid of plethora of legal authorities 
canvassing for a favorable order of reinstatement with full back wages, continuity of service with regularization 
and ancillary benefits from 12.12.2016. As could be heard from Learned Counsel for the opposite party, all these 
wider reliefs sought for by the complainant are the main reliefs claimed in the said case CR 22/2013. By 
consciously avoiding to give oral or documentary evidence in this case, what is craved for on behalf of the 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 93 


complainant is to grant the above reliefs even without facing a trial. Granting such reliefs in his favour without 
providing / supplementing any sort of evidentiary support would tantamount to prejudging the issue raised in the 
Industrial Dispute case CR 22/2013 in a very shortcut method. 


18. Argument is advanced on behalf of the complainant placing reliance upon the verdicts of the Hon'ble High 
Court of Gujarat in Gujarat State Electricity Corporation LTD vs. Bhimrao Aagete (LPA 177 / 2016 dated 
06.03.2018), Kalavatiben Prabhakar Patil and others vs. Managing Director (C/SCA/3189/2020 dated 
17.01.2022) that while deciding a complaint u/s 33A it is not obligatory for the workman to prove that he had 
worked for 240 days. Those rulings in fact do not indicate that the complainant is not at all under obligation to 
substantiate his basic status under the opposite party to justify the case put forth. 


19. In the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case and the very casual manner in which it is manned by the 
complainant, the plethora of rulings relied upon by him viz., Hindustan Lever LTD vs. Ram Mohan Roy and 
others (AIR 1973 SC 1156) by the Hon'ble Apex Court, Management of Karur Vysya Bank LTD vs. 
Presiding Officer, Industrial Tribunal (2007 II LLJ 459) by the Hon'ble High Court of Madras, M M 
Narayana vs. KSRTC (AIR 2012 (4) KAR R 518) and Karan Kumar vs. Divisional Controller KSRTC (WP 
203333/2019 dated 13.07.2023) by the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka and Deutsche Lufthansa AG vs. Nayan 
Pahwa & others (2025 INSC 998) by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi are not of any help to the complainant as 
in all those cases non-compliance of the provisions by the respective employers are relating to regular employees 
on its payroll. Among the cases noted above, the case of Karur Vysya Bank LTD, MM Narayana and Karan 
Kumar are related to the actions initiated by the respective employers based on misconduct / misdemeanor of the 
respective regular employees in respect of which approval applications were not submitted by the employers. In 
the given case though the complainant preferred to contend that his so called retrenchment / termination was 
pursuant to an alleged theft and forging of the cheque leaf of a customer, which factum the opposite part denied 
and disowned, he did not prefer to bring home any reliable evidence to substantiate the said plea. In Hindustan 
Lever’s case also, the complainants were the regular employees of the employer establishment. In principle, the 
fact situations contained in the afore-quoted ruling do not have any application to the case on hand. 


20. Before parting, it is worthy to pen down that in order to avail the relief provided u/s 33 of the Act, firstly the 
aggrieved party should prove himself to be a workman within the definition of u/s 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes 
Act and there exists employer-employee relationship between the contesting parties. In conclusion of the afore- 
discussion, I find that the complainant has miserably failed in substantiating his own case. He equally failed in 
refuting / negating the contentions raised by the opposite party that he is only a coolie engaged on need and 
requirement basis without continuity and frequency and hence not governed by any rules and regulations of the 
bank. So also the complainant further failed in successfully controverting the rival contentions of the opposite 
party that there is no employee-employer relationship between himself and the opposite party or that he was not 
engaged by the latter against a sanctioned post. The deliberate refusal, negligence or avoidance to prove and 
establish a genuine and reliable case by tendering requisite evidence has led the complainant to face a total failure 
in the given case and for an eventual dismissal of the complaint. With this view, these points are answered 
accordingly.

reliefs sought for in this complaint.

The Complaint no. 02/2017 is dismissed.

1. Workman Sh. Baljit Singh has filed the present application directly under Section 2(A)2 of the Industrial 
Dispute Act, 1947 (hereinafter called as the Act) against his termination on 19.01.2015 and praying his reinstatement 
into service with full back wages with continuity in service with all consequential benefits. 


2; The brief facts related to the case are that the workman was appointed by the manager of State Bank of 
India, Koshli as peon w.e.f. 12.07.2009 after completing all formalities and after verifying the bio data submitted by 
him. The Branch Manager assured him that his services would be made permanent and he would be paid full salary 
and allowances as to be paid to the other permanent peon in the bank with all benefits applicable to the post of peon 
as per the service conditions. He was not paid full salary by the branch manager rather a consolidated amount of 
salary was paid per month. He requested many times to the concerned branch manager for regularization of his 
services and payment of full salary also. The workman continued working as peon as well as messenger till 
19.01.2015. 


3. The respondents terminated his services without disclosing any reason without one month notice or pay in 
lieu of notice and without payment of any retrenchment compensation, though he has completed more than five years 
continuously w.e.f. 12.07.2009 to 19.01.2015 without any break and put in more than 240 days of service prior to 
date of his termination. Thus, violated the provisions of Section 25F of the Act. 


4. The respondents also violated the mandatory provisions of Section 25G and 25H of the Act, as juniors have 
been retained in service and fresh hands were engaged by the respondents. 


5. The work and conduct of the workman remained above board during his entire service and there was no 
complaint against him. He used to work about 10 hours daily from 8 AM to 5:45 PM on all working days from 
Monday to Friday and from 8Am to 3:45 PM on Saturday. He was performing all sort of duties, which were to be 
performed by a regular employee, yet he was deprived of all kind of leave, leave travel concession, encashment of 
leave and medical facility and all other benefits, which are available to the regular/permanent employees of the bank. 


6. The workman raised a demand notice regarding his illegal termination from the service by the respondents 
before the Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central) Karnal and upon failure of conciliation proceedings, he filed the 
present claim. It is prayed that he be reinstated in service with full back wages with continuity in service and 
consequential benefits from 19.01.2015 onwards. 


7. Notice of claim was given to the respondents, who filed reply thereof maintaining therein that there is no 
relationship of employer and employee between the workman and respondents. The workman was never appointed by 
the respondent as peon as alleged. There is no post of peon in the bank. The services of applicant were availed by the 
branch manager as a casual labour from time to time on requirement basis. The workman was engaged for the first 
time on 12.07.2009 as daily wager. The workman was never assured by the manager that he will be made permanent 
as there was no post of peon. One Smt. Anita W/o Sanjay of Kosli was an employee of Care Enterprises, who has 
been outsourced by the bank for cleaning the bank premises. The workman was not entitled for regular salary and was 
paid at daily rates for the number of days for which his services were availed by the branch. The workman was 
disengaged when the casual work was not needed. The workman was never appointed by the bank on regular, adhoc 
or temporary basis, hence the provisions of the Act are not attracted in case of workman. The workman did not work

continuously and has not completed 240 days of service prior to date of his termination. No notice pay and 
compensation is required to be paid to the workman as prescribed under Section 25F of the Act. It is prayed that the 
claim may be answered in favor of the respondent and against the workman. 


8. A replication was also filed by the workman rebutting the respondents as has been stated in the written 
statement. 


Evidence of workman:- 


9. In order to prove his case, the workman examined himself as WW 1 and tendered into evidence his affidavit 
WWI1/A and was cross examined by the AR for respondents. The AR for workman closed the evidence on behalf of

10. The respondents examined Sh. Pankaj Yadav, Branch Manager, State Bank of India, Kosli and tendered into

Arguments by parties:- 


12. While arguing the case, AR for workman contended that branch of Kosli was opened on 12.07.2009 and the

19.01.2015. The workman was not paid salary for the period 09/2014 to 12/2014 and he filed application before the

21.07.2015 amounting Rs.30721/-, which include Rs.25371/- as salary for the period 09/2014 to 19.01.2015 @5500/- 
per month and Rs.5350/- as local collection and conveyance charges from 08.11.2014 till 19.01.2015. Thus it is 
proved that workman worked continuously from 12.07.2009 till 19.01.2015 and he was not paid retrenchment

dated 08.01.2015 was written by the Chief Manager to the Branch Manager maintaining therein that fresh workman 
be employed through contractor, which is in violation of Section 25G of the Act. 


13. Even it has been admitted by Sh. Pankaj Yadav MW1 in para no.5 of his affidavit that Smt. Anita W/o Sh. 
Sanjay of Kosli has also been outsourced in place of the workman. AR for workman placed reliance upon judgment 
of Division Bench of Hon'ble Himachal Pradesh High Court in LPA No.258 of 2012 State Bank of India and 
another versus Puja W/o Sh. Makhan Singh in which the Hon'ble High Court has granted relief to the workmen by 
reinstated him along with back wages. Thus, AR for the workman contended that workman be reinstated with full 
back wages. 


14. On the other hand, AR for respondents contended that the workman was purely engaged on daily wage basis 
and he was not entitled for regularization and was not required to give any notice under Section 25F of the Act being 
daily wager. However, it is submitted that he has worked 240 days prior to his termination. He also contended that 
since workman was purely on daily wages, he was not entitled for reinstatement with back wages. To support this 
view, he placed reliance upon case law titled as Jasbir Singh Vs Haryana State Agriculture Marketing Board, 
2009(3) SCT 790 and District Development Officer & Anr. V/s Satish Kantilal Amrelia, Civil Appeal Nos. 19857- 
19858 of 2017; decided on 28 November , 2017. 


Findings:- 
15. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by AR for both the parties. 


16. First this Tribunal is to decide is whether the workman comes within the definition of "workman" as is 
defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. It is mentioned here that applicant was in service of bank w.e.f. 12.07.2009 and 
continuously worked till 19.01.2015 as peon. This fact has been admitted by Mr. Pankaj Yadav MW1 in his cross 
examination in his affidavit that services of the applicant were availed by the branch manager as casual labour for 
menial jobs from time to time on requirement basis of the branch and he was engaged for the first time on 12.07.2009 
as daily wager. Thus workman was not performing the work of regular employee. Even this witness in his cross 
examination has admitted that workman was engaged on 12.07.2009 in Kosli Branch of SBI. He has also admitted 
that entries regarding payment of wages on pages 174 to 176 are correct. It is an admitted fact that there was no peon 
working with the bank and applicant/workman was doing the work as daily wager. In plain words, from the adduced 
evidence, it emerges that he was performing his duty as labourer of unskilled workers. He was not in supervisory or 
administrative post requiring him to perform only administrative post requiring him to perform only administrative 
duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Devinder Singh V/s Municipal Council, 


[भाग --खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 97 


Sanaur AIR 2011 Supreme Court 2532, has observed as follows:- 


"The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms and conditions of employment/contract of 
service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a 
person is a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of Act. The definition of workman also does not make 
any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is 
nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person employed on 
regular basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on 
temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a causal employee or for doing duty for fixed hours 
is not a workman.” 


17. Thus, Hon'ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time or part time or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in employee plain language of 
Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for doing 
whole time job is a workman and the one employed temporary, part time or contract basis or daily wager on fixed 
wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman. In view of the ratio of law 
enunciated in the above ruling, in my considered opinion, the claimant herein admittedly falls within the definition of 
‘workman’ under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


18. Workman has claimed that at the time of his removal, he was getting Rs.5500/- per month and he had 
worked 240 days prior to his termination. As per record placed on file by the respondent, a perusal of page no.176 
and 177 reveals that workman was paid Rs.5000/- and Rs.5500/- as salary, details of which are as under: 


Sr. No. Month Salary paid (in Rupees) 
1. January 2014 5000/- 
2. February 2014 5000/- 
3. April 2014 5500/- 
4. May 2014 5500/- 
5. June 2014 5500/- 
| July 2014 5500/- 
7. August 2014 5500/- 


and thereafter he was paid salary from 09/2014 to 19.01.2015 vide Cheque no.396321542 dated 21.07.2015 
amounting Rs.30721/-, which include Rs.25371/- as salary for the period 09/2014 to 19.01.2015 @5500/- per month 
and Rs.5350/- as local collection and conveyance charges from 08.11.2014 till 19.01.2015. Thus, it emerges that prior 
to his termination from 19.01.2015, he worked 240 days continuously. 


19. Admittedly, the respondent is an industry and there was non- compliance of Section 25-F of the Act and as 
per record, the workman had worked intermittently during the period 12.07.2009 till 19.01.2015 and in place of him 
as per affidavit of MW1, Smt. Anita W/o Sanjay of Kosli was an employee of Care Enterprises which has been 
outsourced by the bank for cleaning the bank premises. Thus, there was violation of Section 25G of the Act. 


20. Admittedly, the respondent is an industry and there was non- compliance of Section 25-F of the Act. The 
workman has already been able to prove that she worked continuously for a period of 240 days prior to her 
termination of her services by respondent on 16.11.2017. It is proved as per statement of Mr. Mohit Dalak, MW1. It 
is added here that the applicant worked as daily wager w.e.f. 12.07.2009 till 19.01.2015 casually. Admittedly, in this 
case, applicant was not paid retrenchment compensation as per Section 25F of the ID Act and in place of him, Smt. 
Anita W/o Sanjay was engaged. Thus, there was violation of Section 25F and 25G of the ID Act. 


21. Admittedly, there is violation of Section 25F of the Act and in view of the judgment of Hon'ble Apex Court 
in Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd.Vs Man Singh, 2012(1) SCT 641, it is not necessary that relief of reinstatement has to 
be given as a matter of right. Reliance can also be placed upon Jasbir Singh Vs Haryana State Agriculture 
Marketing Board (supra), under which it has been held that in the legal position and the Court had recent past, there 
had been a shift in consistently taken the view that relief by way of reinstatement with back wages is not automatic 
and may she wholly inappropriate in a given fact situation, even though termination of an employee was in 


98 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 24, 2026/MAGHA 4, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


contravention of the prescribed procedure. Compensation instead of reinstatement was held to be the prudent relief to 
meet the ends of justice. Moreover, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in case titled as District Development Officer & 


Anr. V/s Satish Kantilal Amrelia (supra), has held as follow: 


"that the reasons for denying the relief of reinstatement in such cases are obvious, It is trite law that when the 
termination is found to be illegal because of non-payment of retrenchment compensation and notice pay as 
mandatorily required under Section 25-F of the Industrial Disputes Act, even after reinstatement, it is always 
open to the management to terminate the services of that employee by paying him the retrenchment 
compensation. Since such a workman was working on daily-wage basis and even after he is reinstated, he has no 
right to seek regularization. Thus he cannot claim regularization and he has no right to continue even as daily- 
wage worker, no useful purpose is going to be served in reinstatement such a workman and he can be given 
monetary compensation by the Court itself inasmuch as if he is terminated again after reinstatement, he would 
receive monetary compensation only in the form of retrenchment compensation and notice pay. In such a 
situation, giving the relief of reinstatement, that too after a long gap, would not serve any purpose". 


In view of facts discussed above workman entitled for compensation as he was working on temporary basis 
intermittently. 


22. Since the workman has stated in his claim that he worked as peon with the management and was getting 
Rs.5500/- per month and was appointed by the Branch Manager. In this regard, it is pertinent to mention here that 
Branch Manager is not appointing authority for appointing the workman. He was not given any appointment letter 
and was daily wager and was not appointed on substantive post. 


23. As regards case law State Bank of India and another versus Puja W/o Sh. Makhan Singh(supra) cited by 


AR for workman is concerned, in that case, bank has concealed facts from the court and has pleaded incorrect stand 
before the court and was held to practicing unfair labour practice. Under these circumstances, the workman was given 
reinstatement. Extract of relevant para 15 of the judgment in above case is reproduced as under:- 


15. Analyzing the facts of instant case, in light of the exposition of law discussed hereinabove, it can safely be 
held to be falling in the zone of exception. The bank being a public sector undertaking was expected to place on 
record true and correct facts. The stand of the bank that workman was not its employee and also having been 
deployed casually, as noticed above, is belied by record and proved otherwise. Considering the incorrect stand 
having been taken by the bank, there is no hesitation to infer unfair labour practice having been applied by the 
bank. 


24. But in the present case, there is no concealment of the facts by the respondent bank. Rather, bank has 
categorically held that workman has worked as daily wager with the bank casually on requirement basis and thus 
under these circumstances, the case of workman is entirely different from the case of State Bank of India and 
another versus Puja W/o Sh. Makhan Singh (supra) relied upon by the AR for workman. Moreover, Hon'ble 


Supreme Court in catena of judgment has held that relief by way of back wages is not automatic and compensation 
instead of reinstatement was held to be the prudent relief to meet the ends of justice. 


25. In view of legal position discussed above, this Court is of the considered view that the workman herein was 
not holding a regular or permanent post nor he was recruited against the post in a regular manner. In such 
circumstances, it is appropriate to grant reasonable compensation instead of reinstatement with back wages. 


26. As such, having due regard to the facts and circumstances, an amount of Rs.2,00,000/- (Rupees Two Lacs) 
appears to be reasonable to which the workman is entitled. In case, the amount of Rs.2,00,000/- (Rupees Two Lacs) 
not paid within one month from the date of publication of the award, the workman is held to be entitled to 6% interet 
from the date of award till payment. File after completion be consigned to the record room. 


27. Let copy of this award be sent to the Appropriate Government as required under Section 17 of the Act for 
publication.

AWARD 


By order No.K-10/1-4/2021-IR Dated: 27.05.2021, the present industrial dispute has been referred for 
adjudication in exercise of the powers conferred by clause (d) of sub-section (1) and sub-section (2A) of Section 10 
the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (14 of 1947) by the Central Government, with following schedule: 


"Whether the action of management of Indian Bank Staff College, Lucknow in terminating the services of 
Shri Ashish Yadav S/O Shri Jagannath Yadav, Receptionist w.e.f. 01.07.2020 who was engaged through 
contractor M/s R.K.Associates, without following the provisions of Section 25 F of I.D. Act, 1947, is Legal 
and justified? If not, to what relief the workman is entitled to and from which date? 


Accordingly, an I.D. Case No. 69/2021 has been registered. 
Thereafter claimant/workman filed a claim statement on 27.05.2021. 


Shri SK Shukla Advocate on behalf of respondent file written statement on 22.04.2022, to which rejoinder affidavit 
has been filed on 24.11.2022. 


Thereafter workman filed his evidence on affidavit (Examination in Chief) on 07.06.2023. 


From the perusal of the record it transpired that in spite of repeated opportunity given to the workman, Shri Ashish 
Yadav who has filed evidence on affidavit (Examination in chief) does not turn up for his cross examination. 


So by order dated 14.03.2024, right to get him cross examine (Shri Ashish yadav/workman) was closed. 


Thereafter on 22.11.2024, an application moved for recall of the order dated 14.03.2024, supported by affidavit, titled 
as “APPLICATION FOR RECALL OF ORDER DATED 14.03.2024”. 


Further time was granted to the claimant/workman to press the same. 


However none appeared on behalf of workman to press the same, so by order dated 23.01.2025, application for recall 
of order dated 14.03.2024, moved on 22.11.2024 by claimant/workman was rejected. 


Further perusal from record the position which emerged out, on 03.10.2025 the matter was fixed for ex parte hearing 
and notice was send to claimant/workman. 


As none appeared on behalf of the workman, so the matter was adjourned and one more opportunity was granted to 


100 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 24, 2026/MAGHA 4, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


workman, and matter was fixed for ex parte hearing on 25.11.2025, notice was send to him. 


In spite of the said facts i.e. service of the notice for proceeding ex parte, today when the matter listed for hearing, 
none appeared on behalf of the workman. 


Shri SK Shukla learned counsel for respondent has appeared. 
Ihave heard Shri SK Shukla Advocate for respondent and perused the record. 


Keeping in view the above said facts, this is a case of no evidence because worker did not cross examined himself on 
the evidence filed by him on affidavit (examination in chief) so the same in not proved as per the relevant provision 
Evidence Act, so keeping the said facts and the law as laid by the Hon'ble High Court in the case of V. K. Raj 
Industries v. Labour Court (1) and others 1981 (29) FLR 194 as under: 


"It is well settled that if a party challenges the legality of an order, the burden lies upon him to prove 
illegality of the order and if no evidence is produced the party invoking jurisdiction of the Court must fail 
Whenever a workman raises a dispute challenging the validity of the termination of service if is imperative 
for him to file written statement before the Industrial Court setting out grounds on which the order is 
challenged and he must also produce evidence to prove his case. If the workman fails to appear or to file 
written statement or produce evidence, the dispute referred by the State Government cannot be answered in 
favour of the workman and he would not be entitled to any relief." 


In the case of M/s Uptron Powertronics Employees' Union, Ghaziabad through its Secretary v. Presiding 
Officer, Labour Court (IID, Ghaziabad and others 2008 (118) FLR 1164 Hon'ble Allahabad High Court has held 
as under: 


"The law has been settled by the Apex Court in case of Shanker Chakravarti v. Britannia Biscuit Co. Ltd., 
V.K. Raj Industries v. Labour Court and Ors., Airtech Private Limited v. State of U.P. and Ors. 1984 (49) 
FLR 38 and Meritech India Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Ors. 1996 FLR that in the absence of any evidence led 
by or on behalf of the workman the reference is bound to be answered by the court against the workman. In 
such a situation it is not necessary for the employers to lead any evidence at all. The obligation to lead 
evidence to establish an allegation made by a party is on the party making the allegation. The test would be, 
who would fail if no evidence is led." 


And by the Hon'ble Allahabad High Court in the case of District Administrative Committee, U.P. P.A.C.C.S.C. 
Services v. Secretary-cum-G.M. District Co- operative Bank Ltd. 2010 (126) FLR 519; wherein it has been held 
as under: 


"The submission is that even if the petitioner failed to lead the evidence, burden was on the shoulders of the 
respondent to prove the termination order as illegal. He was required to lead evidence first which he failed. 
A perusal of the impugned award also does not show that any evidence either oral or documentary was led 
by the respondent. In the case of no evidence, the reference has to be dismissed." 


AWARD 
For the foregoing reasons, the case is dismissed and; and the workman is not entitled for any relief. 
Award as above.

have referred a dispute between the Management of UCO Bank, Begedia Branch and allegedly its workmen vide

Bagadia branch of UCO Bank had terminated her services without any prior notice resulting financial loss and mental

That, the 2" party is not a “workman” of the management-Bank and there was no “employer and employee”

industrial dispute exists in this case. The 2™ party is not a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, so the present reference is bad in law. The services of the 2" party-work-woman Smt.

days she had worked in the Bank. Moreover, the Bank has never issued any appointment letter or termination letter to 
the workwoman, so the compliance of Section 25-F of the ID. Act does not arise in this case. She had never 
completed continuous service in the Bank for more than 240 days in a year preceding to her termination. The 27 party 
workwoman after the death of her husband had approached the Branch Manager of the Bagadia Branch of UCO Bank 
for providing her some part time miscellaneous work and the Branch Manager on humanitarian ground offered her 
some miscellaneous work as and when required. The 2™ party-work-woman was not an employee of the Bank so she 
had not marked her presence in the attendance register and she had never worked continuously in any year of her 
contractual engagement continuously and uninterruptedly. The Management-Bank is not under any obligation to 
serve any notice and no illegal & arbitrary action had been taken by the Management against her. 


A prayer has been made by the 1‘ Party-Management to dismiss __ the claim of the 2™ party-work-woman as 
she is not entitled for any __ relief.

denying all the averments made by the 17 Party-Management.

ISSUES

ii) Whether any action of the management of UCO Bank, Bagadia Branch, Dist. Angul, Odisha in terminating 
Smt. Kalpana Pradhan w.e.f. 19.01.2016 without assigning any reason and without following the provisions 
of I.D. Act, 1947 is legal & Justified?

7. The 2™ party-workman has examined only one witness. She is the workwoman herself Kalpana Pradhan as 
W.W.-1 and she has proved _ the following documents which are marked as hereunder:-

Asst. Manager, UCO Bank, Bagadia Branch of Angul. 


9: In course of his evidence he has proved the following documents which are marked as :-

FINDINGS 
ISSUE NO. 1 & I 
10. Both the issues are taken up together for the sake of convenience. 
11. At the outset of discussions it is required to mention here that it is an admitted fact that late Saudagar 


Pradhan, husband of the 21 party-work-work-woman was a sub-staff of the Management-Bank at Bagadia Branch 
and he died on 24.04.2010. Further it is also admitted fact that after the death of late Saudagar Pradhan his wife 2" 
party workwoman was engaged by the Management-Bank occasionally as and when basis. 


12. It is the case of the 2" Party-workman that after the death of late Saudagar Pradhan, his wife Kalpana 
Pradhan was employed as a daily labourer since 26.04.2010 till 19.01.2016. However, the 1“ Party-Management has 
denied that the 2™ party-work-woman was engaged on daily wage basis regularly. 


13. Now in the light of the above discussions, the Tribunal thinks it proper to discuss the oral and documentary 
evidence available in the record. 


14. The most competent witness in this case is W.W.-1. Smt. Kalpana Pradhan who has fully supported her case 
in the evidence. She has categorically deposed that she was employed as a daily 1 abourer with effect from 
26.04.2010 on post of her husband under the Management and she performed her duty continuously and 
uninterruptedly under the 17 Party-Management till the date of her illegal termination. She has also stated 
that during her service tenure her work was fixed from 9.30 A.M. till closure of the Bank and she was paid monthly 
salary by the Management on the first week of the subsequent month by signing on cash vouchers on the head

Section 2(00) of the I.D. Act reads as follows:- 


Section 2(00) -“retrenchment” means the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for

25-B. Definition of continuous service — For the purpose of —_ this Chapter,- 


(1) a workman shall be said to be in continuous service for a period if he is, for that period, in 
uninterrupted service, including service which may be interrupted on account of sickness or

which is not due to any fault on the part of the workman;

year or six months, 16 shall be deemed to be in continuous service under an employer-

“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of

13. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make 
any distinction between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is 
nothing in plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular 
basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, 
part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a 
workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the above ruling, in my considered opinion the claimant 
herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under Section 2(s) of the Act.

1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and
