of being so expressed which would if the terms of employment, expressed or employed were fulfilled be payable to 
person employed in respect of his employer or of work done in such employer and includes. 


(d) Any sum which by reason of termination of employment of the person employed is payable under any law 
contract or instrument which provides for the payment of such sum whether with nor without deduction but does not 
provide for the time within which the payment is to be made. 


Thus, in view of the above definition of wages the retrenchment allowances are very much covered under the 
definition of wages and the contention of the Respondent No.1 that retrenchment allowances are not included under 
the wages is untenable. According to Ex. W12 the term of payment/mode of payment has been agreed upon between 
Respondent No.2 the main contractor and Respondent No.3 sub-contractor, to be paid to the contract Labour i.e. 
Petitioner for doing the work at Respondent No.1 industry. The employment of Petitioner by Respondent No.3 of the 
Petitioner has been admitted by Respondent No. | & 2 and it is also admitted that retrenchment allowances of the 
Petitioner workman has not been paid by none of the Respondents. Therefore, as a Principal Employer Respondent 
No.1 is liable to pay retrenchment allowance to the Petitioner in view of the provision contained under Section 21 (4) 
of Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 and he may recover the said amount of retrenchment 
allowances so paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 2 and Respondent No. 3. Thus, the contention of Respondent 
No. | in this context is untenable. 


18. Therefore, in view of foregone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed in preceding 
paragraph of this order, I come to irresistible conclusion that as per document Ex. W8 and W12 Petitioner had worked 
with the Respondent No. 1 as contract labour employed by Respondent No.3 as sub-contractor of Respondent No.2, 
during the period from 16-08-2009 to 15-08-2012 and Respondent No.3 the employer has terminated the services of 
Petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012. Therefore, Petitioner is entitled for payment of retrenchment allowances as per 
document Ex. W12 which has been proved by the oral and documentary evidence of Petitioner and also admitted by 
Respondent No. 3 it is undisputed that none of the Respondents has paid such retrenchment allowance to the 
Petitioner. Therefore, as per provision contained under section 21 (4) of contract labour (Regulation and Abolition) 
Act, 1970 the Respondent No. 1 being principal employer is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowance to 
Petitioner, and he may recover said amount paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. | and 2 jointly and severally. 
Thus, the Petition filed by the Petitioner has merits and deserved to be allowed. 


ORDER 
The Petition filed by the Petitioner under section 33C(2) of ID Act 1947 is allowed.

hereunder: - 


(a) In the case of Sail Growth Works versus Nilmani Lal and others, Writ Petition Number 386 of 2025, dated 10" 
March 2025, the Hon’ble High Court of Kolkata has held: 


19. Gratuity, payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, is a gratuitous payment required to be 
made by an employer to his employee at the time of termination of services of the employee or upon such 
employee’s death. 


Section 21 (4) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA), mandates that a 
principal employer is responsible for the payment of 'wages' to a contract employee in the event of a contractor's 
failure to pay within the stipulated timelines or in the event of a contractor making a short payment. The principal 
employer then has the ability to recover the amount paid as ‘wages’, from the contractor. Section 2(h) of the CLRA 
defines the term 'wages' as all remuneration (whether by salary, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of 
money or capable of being so expressed, which would if the terms of employment, expressed or implied, were 
fulfilled, be payable to a person employed in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment and

includes, among others, (६) any sum which by reason of the termination of employment of the person employed is 
payable under any law, contract or instrument which provides for the payment..."". However, it excludes (6) any 
gratuity payable on the termination of employees in cases other than those specified in (d)."" In Superintending 
Engineer, Mettur Thermal Power Station, Mettur vs. Appellate Page 11 Authority, Joint Commissioner of Labour, 
Coimbatore & Anr, 2012 LLR 1160, it has been held by the Madras High Court that gratuity payable under the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 falls within this definition of 'wages'. The principal employer or the contractor may 
be liable to pay gratuity to contract employees, depending on the circumstances. Principal employer The principal 
employer is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if the contractor fails to pay. The principal employer is 
liable to pay gratuity if the contractor makes a short payment. 


The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contractor terminates the services of the contract 
employee. The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contract employee works for multiple contractors. 
Contractor The contractor is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if they have worked for at least five years 
and the contract is separate from the company. 


(b) In the case of Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited versus Commissioner of Labour, Appeal Civil 
Number 11355 of 1996, dated 37 September 1996, the Hon’ble Court have held: - 


“The short question that arises for determination is whether the appellant who the principal employer is liable to 
pay to the contract workers any amount which constitutes the difference between the wages payable to the contract 
labour by the contractor and the wages paid by the appellant to its own employees doing similar work. The Division 
Bench seems to have relied upon Section 21(4) of the said Act for this purpose. Section 21(1), however, provides 
that the contractor shall be responsible for the payment of wages to each worker employed by his. Section 21(4) 
provides that if the contractor fails to make this payment or any part thereof, the principal employer is liable to 
make this payment and may recover the same from the contractor as set out in that sub-section. Looking to the 
definition of wages Under the said Act read with the definition of wages in the payment of Wages Act, which we 
have set out earlier, it is clear that Section 21 only deals with the payment of contractual wages by the contractor to 
each of his worker; The definition of wages would cover within its scope, inter alia, also those amounts which the 
contractor is liable to pay his workers under any award, settlement or order of court as well as other amounts 
falling within the definition of wages under the payment of Wages Act Subjection (2) provides for a representative 
of the principal employer supervising this payment. Clearly, therefore, the wages which are the subject-matter of 
Section 21 are specified sums which are payable in present by the contractor under the terms of his contract of 
employment with each worker as well as under any existing award, settlement or order of the court. -Section 21 
does not deal with, nor does if cover the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Rules, 1971. Hence Section 
21(4) will not apply to such obligations of the contractor which may be the subject-matter of dispute between the 
contractor and his workers at time of disbursement of wages and which do not fall within the definition of “wages” 
under the Act.” 


(c) Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Bombay Industries Chemical Industries Vs Deputy 
Labour Commissioner, Civil Appeal Number 813 of 2022, D.O.D dated 4" February 2022, the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court has held that the benefit sought to be enforced under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a pre-existing 
benefit or one flowing from a pre-existing right. The Hon’ble Court added that in the case of Kanku Ben, it is 
observed and held that whenever a workman is entitled to receive from his employer any money or any benefit which 
is capable of being computed in terms of money and which he is entitled to receive from his employer and is denied 
of such benefit can approach Labour Court Under section 33-C(2) of the ID Act. It is further observed that the benefit 
sought to be enforced Under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a preexisting benefit or one flowing from a 
preexisting right. The difference between a preexisting right or benefit on one hand and the right or benefit, which is 
considered just and fair on the other hand is vital. The former falls within jurisdiction of Labour Court exercising 
powers under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act, while the latter does not. 


(d) In the case of Jeet Lal Sharma versus Presiding Officer, 2001 VAD Delhi One, dated 157 March 2000, the 
Hon’ble High Court of Delhi have held:- 


“15. The point which is emphasised is that entitlement to receive money the pre-existing right can the 
based on (1) adjudication (2) settlement (3) service conditions. If the right to get a particular benefit is there, the 
application us. 13-C(2) would be maintainable and jurisdiction of Labour Court will not be barred merely because 
employer has denied the same

right. However where the workman claims a benefit flowing from a pre-existing right and approaches the Labour 
Courts 33-612) for computation of the right in term of money and the employer disputes the existences of the right,

of right is established than in proceed in compute the benefit flowing therefrom in terms of money or on its 
decisions recovery proceedings start (New Taj Mahal Cafe Private Limited versus Labour Court reported in 1970 
(2) LLN 51 and East India Coal Company Limited (supra) In deciding the maintainability of the application u/s 
13-(12) what is in be looked at is the clans set up in the application and not what the other side contends in its

contract of employment between the employer and the stipulation in that behalf 
contained therein; or” 


Although Petitioner might be working with Respondent No.1 even after 15.08.2012 but Respondent No.3 is no more 
employer of workman. Therefore, only conclusion can be drawn in such circumstances that Respondent No. 3 has 
terminated the service of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. Thus, Petitioner is entitled to receive retrenchment/allowance as 
per Ex. W12. Thus, the contention of R3 in this context is untenable. Therefore, the plea of Petitioner that Petitioner 
worker is working now under new contractor is untenable as the Respondent No. 3 is no more employer of the 
Petitioner after 15-08-2012 meaning thereby Petitioner has been terminated by Respondent No. 3 from service w.e.f 
16.08.2012 and is entitled to receive retrenchment allowances as per terns of the contract. 


17. | However, Respondent No. 1 has contended that terminal benefits claimed by the Petitioner do not form part of 
wages and as such the contractor as direct employer is responsible to make all other payments. In this context, the 
reference of definition of wages u/s 2 (IV) Payment of Wages Act, 1936 is relevant. Therein it is provided that wages 
mean all remuneration (whether by way of salaries, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of money are capable 
of being so expressed which would if the terms of employment, expressed or employed were fulfilled be payable to 
person employed in respect of his employer or of work done in such employer and includes. 


(d) Any sum which by reason of termination of employment of the person employed is payable under any law 
contract or instrument which provides for the payment of such sum whether with nor without deduction but does not 
provide for the time within which the payment is to be made. 


Thus, in view of the above definition of wages the retrenchment allowances are very much covered under the 
definition of wages and the contention of the Respondent No.1 that retrenchment allowances are not included under 
the wages is untenable. According to Ex. W12 the term of payment/mode of payment has been agreed upon between 
Respondent No.2 the main contractor and Respondent No.3 sub-contractor, to be paid to the contract Labour i.e. 
Petitioner for doing the work at Respondent No.1! industry. The employment of Petitioner by Respondent No.3 of the 
Petitioner has been admitted by Respondent No. | & 2 and it is also admitted that retrenchment allowances of the 
Petitioner workman has not been paid by none of the Respondents. Therefore, as a Principal Employer Respondent 
No.1 is liable to pay retrenchment allowance to the Petitioner in view of the provision contained under Section 21 (4) 
of Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 and he may recover the said amount of retrenchment 
allowances so paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 2 and Respondent No. 3. Thus, the contention of Respondent 
No. | in this context is untenable. 


18. Therefore, in view of foregone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed in preceding 
paragraph of this order, I come to irresistible conclusion that as per document Ex. W8 and W12 Petitioner had worked

with the Respondent No. 1 as contract labour employed by Respondent No.3 as sub-contractor of Respondent No.2, 
during the period from 16-08-2009 to 15-08-2012 and Respondent No.3 the employer has terminated the services of 
Petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012. Therefore, Petitioner is entitled for payment of retrenchment allowances as per 
document Ex. W12 which has been proved by the oral and documentary evidence of Petitioner and also admitted by 
Respondent No. 3 it is undisputed that none of the Respondents has paid such retrenchment allowance to the 
Petitioner. Therefore, as per provision contained under section 21 (4) of contract labour (Regulation and Abolition) 
Act, 1970 the Respondent No. 1 being principal employer is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowance to 
Petitioner, and he may recover said amount paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 1 and 2 jointly and severally. 
Thus, the Petition filed by the Petitioner has merits and deserved to be allowed.

15. In this context, relevant decisions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Court, are discussed as 
hereunder: - 


(a) In the case of Sail Growth Works versus Nilmani Lal and others, Writ Petition Number 386 of 2025, dated 10" 
March 2025, the Hon’ble High Court of Kolkata has held: 


19. Gratuity, payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, is a gratuitous payment required to be 
made by an employer to his employee at the time of termination of services of the employee or upon such 
employee’s death. 


Section 21 (4) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA), mandates that a 
principal employer is responsible for the payment of 'wages' to a contract employee in the event of a contractor's 
failure to pay within the stipulated timelines or in the event of a contractor making a short payment. The principal 
employer then has the ability to recover the amount paid as 'wages', from the contractor. Section 2(h) of the CLRA 
defines the term 'wages' as all remuneration (whether by salary, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of 
money or capable of being so expressed, which would if the terms of employment, expressed or implied, were 
fulfilled, be payable to a person employed in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment and 
includes, among others, ''(d) any sum which by reason of the termination of employment of the person employed is 
payable under any law, contract or instrument which provides for the payment..."". However, it excludes (6) any 
gratuity payable on the termination of employees in cases other than those specified in (d)."" In Superintending 
Engineer, Mettur Thermal Power Station, Mettur vs. Appellate Page 11 Authority, Joint Commissioner of Labour, 
Coimbatore & Anr, 2012 LLR 1160, it has been held by the Madras High Court that gratuity payable under the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 falls within this definition of 'wages'. The principal employer or the contractor may 
be liable to pay gratuity to contract employees, depending on the circumstances. Principal employer The principal

employer is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if the contractor fails to pay. The principal employer is 
liable to pay gratuity if the contractor makes a short payment. 


The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contractor terminates the services of the contract 
employee. The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contract employee works for multiple contractors. 
Contractor The contractor is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if they have worked for at least five years 
and the contract is separate from the company. 


(b) In the case of Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited versus Commissioner of Labour, Appeal Civil 
Number 11355 of 1996, dated 37 September 1996, the Hon’ble Court have held: - 


“The short question that arises for determination is whether the appellant who the principal employer is liable to 
pay to the contract workers any amount which constitutes the difference between the wages payable to the contract 
labour by the contractor and the wages paid by the appellant to its own employees doing similar work. The Division 
Bench seems to have relied upon Section 21(4) of the said Act for this purpose. Section 21(1), however, provides 
that the contractor shall be responsible for the payment of wages to each worker employed by his. Section 21(4) 
provides that if the contractor fails to make this payment or any part thereof, the principal employer is liable to 
make this payment and may recover the same from the contractor as set out in that sub-section. Looking to the 
definition of wages Under the said Act read with the definition of wages in the payment of Wages Act, which we 
have set out earlier, it is clear that Section 21 only deals with the payment of contractual wages by the contractor to 
each of his worker; The definition of wages would cover within its scope, inter alia, also those amounts which the 
contractor is liable to pay his workers under any award, settlement or order of court as well as other amounts 
falling within the definition of wages under the payment of Wages Act Subjection (2) provides for a representative 
of the principal employer supervising this payment. Clearly, therefore, the wages which are the subject-matter of 
Section 21 are specified sums which are payable in present by the contractor under the terms of his contract of 
employment with each worker as well as under any existing award, settlement or order of the court. -Section 21 
does not deal with, nor does if cover the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Rules, 1971. Hence Section 
21(4) will not apply to such obligations of the contractor which may be the subject-matter of dispute between the 
contractor and his workers at time of disbursement of wages and which do not fall within the definition of “wages” 
under the Act.” 


(c) Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Bombay Industries Chemical Industries Vs Deputy 
Labour Commissioner, Civil Appeal Number 813 of 2022, D.O.D dated 4" February 2022, the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court has held that the benefit sought to be enforced under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a pre-existing 
benefit or one flowing from a pre-existing right. The Hon’ble Court added that in the case of Kanku Ben, it is 
observed and held that whenever a workman is entitled to receive from his employer any money or any benefit which 
is capable of being computed in terms of money and which he is entitled to receive from his employer and is denied 
of such benefit can approach Labour Court Under section 33-C(2) of the ID Act. It is further observed that the benefit 
sought to be enforced Under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a preexisting benefit or one flowing from a 
preexisting right. The difference between a preexisting right or benefit on one hand and the right or benefit, which is 
considered just and fair on the other hand is vital. The former falls within jurisdiction of Labour Court exercising 
powers under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act, while the latter does not. 


(d) In the case of Jeet Lal Sharma versus Presiding Officer, 2001 VAD Delhi One, dated 157 March 2000, the 
Hon’ble High Court of Delhi have held:- 


“15. The point which is emphasised is that entitlement to receive money the pre-existing right can the 
based on (1) adjudication (2) settlement (3) service conditions. If the right to get a particular benefit is there, the 
application us. 13-C(2) would be maintainable and jurisdiction of Labour Court will not be barred merely because 
employer has denied the same 


16. What is the meaning of the expression "entitlement in receive". No doubt it is referable to pre-existing 
right. However where the workman claims a benefit flowing from a pre-existing right and approaches the Labour 
Courts 33-612) for computation of the right in term of money and the employer disputes the existences of the right, 
the Labour Court will have the jurisdiction to determine the question, whether the right exists and if the existence 
of right is established than in proceed in compute the benefit flowing therefrom in terms of money or on its 
decisions recovery proceedings start (New Taj Mahal Cafe Private Limited versus Labour Court reported in 1970 
(2) LLN 51 and East India Coal Company Limited (supra) In deciding the maintainability of the application u/s 
13-(12) what is in be looked at is the clans set up in the application and not what the other side contends in its 
reply. The fact that the employer by his plea rises some dispute, does not mean that Jurisdiction of Labour Court to 
deal with the question is taken away.” 


16. Thus, in view of forgone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed above, Petition filed by the 
Petitioner under Section 33-C(2) of ID Act,1947 against the Respondents for recovery of retrenchment allowances as 
per Ex. W12 is acceptable. Undisputedly, Petitioner was engaged by Respondent No.3 M/s Rishitha Associates, and 
Respondent No.2 has engaged Respondent No. 3 as sub-contractor for Labour supply to work in the establishment of

The definition of retrenchment as provided under Section 2 (00) is extracted as here under: - 


2(00) “retrenchment “means the termination by the employer f the service of a workman for any reason 
whatsoever, otherwise than as punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action but does not include--- 


(a) Voluntary retirement of the workman: or 


(b) Retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract

stipulation in that behalf; or 


(bb) termination of the service of the workman as a result of the non-renewal of the 
contract of employment between the employer and the stipulation in that behalf 
contained therein; or” 


Although Petitioner might be working with Respondent No.1 even after 15.08.2012 but Respondent No.3 is no more 
employer of workman. Therefore, only conclusion can be drawn in such circumstances that Respondent No. 3 has

17. | However, Respondent No. 1 has contended that terminal benefits claimed by the Petitioner do not form part of 
wages and as such the contractor as direct employer is responsible to make all other payments. In this context, the 
reference of definition of wages u/s 2 (19७) Payment of Wages Act, 1936 is relevant. Therein it is provided that wages 
mean all remuneration (whether by way of salaries, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of money are capable 
of being so expressed which would if the terms of employment, expressed or employed were fulfilled be payable to 
person employed in respect of his employer or of work done in such employer and includes. 


(d) Any sum which by reason of termination of employment of the person employed is payable under any law 
contract or instrument which provides for the payment of such sum whether with nor without deduction but does not 
provide for the time within which the payment is to be made. 


Thus, in view of the above definition of wages the retrenchment allowances are very much covered under the

18. Therefore, in view of foregone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed in preceding

with the Respondent No. 1 as contract labour employed by Respondent No.3 as sub-contractor of Respondent No.2,

Firstly, we have to examine provision contained under section 33 C (2) of the ID Act. Section 33 C (2) of ID Act 
provides :- 


"Where any workman is entitled to receive from the employer any money or any benefit which is capable 
of being computed in terms of money, and if any question arises as to the amount of money due or as to 
the amount at which such benefit should be computed, then the question may, subject to any rules that 
may be wait under this act, be decided by such labour court as may be specified in this behalf by the 
appropriate government within a period of not exceeding three month."

15. In this context, relevant decisions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Court, are discussed as 
hereunder: - 


(a) In the case of Sail Growth Works versus Nilmani Lal and others, Writ Petition Number 386 of 2025, dated 
107 March 2025, the Hon’ble High Court of Kolkata has held: 


19. Gratuity, payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, is a gratuitous payment required to be 
made by an employer to his employee at the time of termination of services of the employee or upon such 
employee’s death. 


Section 21 (4) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA), mandates that a 
principal employer is responsible for the payment of 'wages' to a contract employee in the event of a contractor's 
failure to pay within the stipulated timelines or in the event of a contractor making a short payment. The principal 
employer then has the ability to recover the amount paid as ‘wages’, from the contractor. Section 2(h) of the CLRA 
defines the term 'wages' as all remuneration (whether by salary, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of 
money or capable of being so expressed, which would if the terms of employment, expressed or implied, were 
fulfilled, be payable to a person employed in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment and 
includes, among others, (६) any sum which by reason of the termination of employment of the person employed is 
payable under any law, contract or instrument which provides for the payment..."". However, it excludes (6) any 
gratuity payable on the termination of employees in cases other than those specified in (d)."" In Superintending 
Engineer, Mettur Thermal Power Station, Mettur vs. Appellate Page 11 Authority, Joint Commissioner of Labour, 
Coimbatore & Anr, 2012 LLR 1160, it has been held by the Madras High Court that gratuity payable under the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 falls within this definition of 'wages'. The principal employer or the contractor may

be liable to pay gratuity to contract employees, depending on the circumstances. Principal employer The principal 
employer is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if the contractor fails to pay. The principal employer is 
liable to pay gratuity if the contractor makes a short payment. 


The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contractor terminates the services of the contract 
employee. The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contract employee works for multiple contractors. 
Contractor The contractor is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if they have worked for at least five years 
and the contract is separate from the company. 


(b) In the case of Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited versus Commissioner of Labour, Appeal Civil 
Number 11355 of 1996, dated 37 September 1996, the Hon’ble Court have held: - 


“The short question that arises for determination is whether the appellant who the principal employer is liable to 
pay to the contract workers any amount which constitutes the difference between the wages payable to the contract 
labour by the contractor and the wages paid by the appellant to its own employees doing similar work. The Division 
Bench seems to have relied upon Section 21(4) of the said Act for this purpose. Section 21(1), however, provides 
that the contractor shall be responsible for the payment of wages to each worker employed by his. Section 21(4) 
provides that if the contractor fails to make this payment or any part thereof, the principal employer is liable to 
make this payment and may recover the same from the contractor as set out in that sub-section. Looking to the 
definition of wages Under the said Act read with the definition of wages in the payment of Wages Act, which we 
have set out earlier, it is clear that Section 21 only deals with the payment of contractual wages by the contractor to 
each of his worker; The definition of wages would cover within its scope, inter alia, also those amounts which the 
contractor is liable to pay his workers under any award, settlement or order of court as well as other amounts 
falling within the definition of wages under the payment of Wages Act Subjection (2) provides for a representative 
of the principal employer supervising this payment. Clearly, therefore, the wages which are the subject-matter of 
Section 21 are specified sums which are payable in present by the contractor under the terms of his contract of 
employment with each worker as well as under any existing award, settlement or order of the court. -Section 21 
does not deal with, nor does if cover the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Rules, 1971. Hence Section 
21(4) will not apply to such obligations of the contractor which may be the subject-matter of dispute between the 
contractor and his workers at time of disbursement of wages and which do not fall within the definition of “wages” 
under the Act.” 


(c) Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Bombay Industries Chemical Industries Vs Deputy 
Labour Commissioner, Civil Appeal Number 813 of 2022, D.O.D dated 4" February 2022, the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court has held that the benefit sought to be enforced under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a pre-existing 
benefit or one flowing from a pre-existing right. The Hon’ble Court added that in the case of Kanku Ben, it is 
observed and held that whenever a workman is entitled to receive from his employer any money or any benefit which 
is capable of being computed in terms of money and which he is entitled to receive from his employer and is denied 
of such benefit can approach Labour Court Under section 33-C(2) of the ID Act. It is further observed that the benefit 
sought to be enforced Under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a preexisting benefit or one flowing from a 
preexisting right. The difference between a preexisting right or benefit on one hand and the right or benefit, which is 
considered just and fair on the other hand is vital. The former falls within jurisdiction of Labour Court exercising 
powers under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act, while the latter does not. 


(d) In the case of Jeet Lal Sharma versus Presiding Officer, 2001 VAD Delhi One, dated 157 March 2000, the 
Hon’ble High Court of Delhi have held:- 


“15. The point which is emphasised is that entitlement to receive money the pre-existing right can the 
based on (1) adjudication (2) settlement (3) service conditions. If the right to get a particular benefit is there, the 
application us. 13-C(2) would be maintainable and jurisdiction of Labour Court will not be barred merely because 
employer has denied the same 


16. What is the meaning of the expression "entitlement in receive". No doubt it is referable to pre-existing 
right. However where the workman claims a benefit flowing from a pre-existing right and approaches the Labour 
Courts 33-612) for computation of the right in term of money and the employer disputes the existences of the right, 
the Labour Court will have the jurisdiction to determine the question, whether the right exists and if the existence 
of right is established than in proceed in compute the benefit flowing therefrom in terms of money or on its 
decisions recovery proceedings start (New Taj Mahal Cafe Private Limited versus Labour Court reported in 1970 
(2) LLN 51 and East India Coal Company Limited (supra) In deciding the maintainability of the application u/s 
13-(12) what is in be looked at is the clans set up in the application and not what the other side contends in its 
reply. The fact that the employer by his plea rises some dispute, does not mean that Jurisdiction of Labour Court to 
deal with the question is taken away.”

appropriate government within a period of not exceeding three month."

14. Now, question arises that who is liable to pay the said retrenchment allowances to the Petitioner as per 
contract. Admittedly, Petitioner workman was engaged by Respondent No.3 for the work of Respondent No.1. 
Respondent No.1 has admitted that the Petitioner had worked in the work of Strapping Mills Products WRM in its 
industry during the period from 16.8.2009 to 15.8.2012 as contract labour engaged by Respondent No.3. Since the 
Respondent No. 3 was sub-contractor for labour supply for the work order Ex. W8 of Respondent No.2, therefore, 
Respondent No.1, Respondent No.2 and Respondent No.3 are jointly and severally liable to pay retrenchment 
allowances towards the full and final payment to the Petitioner as per contract. Although Respondent No.3 contended 
that it has paid all the money due to the Petitioner, but Respondent No.3 has not produced any document to establish 
that full and final payment as claimed by the Petitioner towards retrenchment allowances has been paid by 2" 
Respondent or 37 Respondent. However, Respondent has filed photocopies of documents as proof of payment to the 
workman by R-2. The perusal of these photocopies goes to show that these are not proved by any cogent and relevant 
evidence of witness. Therefore, these photocopies in respect of payment are not admissible in evidence. Moreover, 
the genuineness of these document photocopies has been challenged by the Petitioner in his rejoinder, therefore, 
burden of proof to prove the factum of payment to the Petitioner lies on the Respondent No.1 which he failed to 
discharge. Thus, it is established that Petitioner is entitled to receive the amount towards benefits upon his 
retrenchment from service by R-3. Moreover, Respondent No.1 is the Principal Employer of Petitioner contract 
labour, therefore, Respondent No.1 is also liable to pay retrenchment allowances to Petitioner along with Respondent 
No.2 and Respondent No.3 jointly and severally.

(a) In the case of Sail Growth Works versus Nilmani Lal and others, Writ Petition Number 386 of 2025, dated 10" 
March 2025, the Hon’ble High Court of Kolkata has held: 


19. Gratuity, payable under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, is a gratuitous payment required to be 
made by an employer to his employee at the time of termination of services of the employee or upon such 
employee’s death. 


Section 21 (4) of the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (CLRA), mandates that a 
principal employer is responsible for the payment of 'wages' to a contract employee in the event of a contractor's 
failure to pay within the stipulated timelines or in the event of a contractor making a short payment. The principal 
employer then has the ability to recover the amount paid as ‘wages’, from the contractor. Section 2(h) of the CLRA 
defines the term 'wages' as all remuneration (whether by salary, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of 
money or capable of being so expressed, which would if the terms of employment, expressed or implied, were 
fulfilled, be payable to a person employed in respect of his employment or of work done in such employment and 
includes, among others, ''(d) any sum which by reason of the termination of employment of the person employed is 
payable under any law, contract or instrument which provides for the payment..."". However, it excludes (6) any 
gratuity payable on the termination of employees in cases other than those specified in (d)."" In Superintending 
Engineer, Mettur Thermal Power Station, Mettur vs. Appellate Page 11 Authority, Joint Commissioner of Labour, 
Coimbatore & Anr, 2012 LLR 1160, it has been held by the Madras High Court that gratuity payable under the 
Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 falls within this definition of 'wages'. The principal employer or the contractor may 
be liable to pay gratuity to contract employees, depending on the circumstances. Principal employer The principal 
employer is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if the contractor fails to pay. The principal employer is 


[भाग --खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 523 


liable to pay gratuity if the contractor makes a short payment. 


The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contractor terminates the services of the contract 
employee. The principal employer is liable to pay gratuity if the contract employee works for multiple contractors. 
Contractor The contractor is liable to pay gratuity to contract employees if they have worked for at least five years 
and the contract is separate from the company. 


(b) In the case of Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited versus Commissioner of Labour, Appeal Civil 
Number 11355 of 1996, dated 37 September 1996, the Hon’ble Court have held: - 


“The short question that arises for determination is whether the appellant who the principal employer is liable to 
pay to the contract workers any amount which constitutes the difference between the wages payable to the contract 
labour by the contractor and the wages paid by the appellant to its own employees doing similar work. The Division 
Bench seems to have relied upon Section 21(4) of the said Act for this purpose. Section 21(1), however, provides 
that the contractor shall be responsible for the payment of wages to each worker employed by his. Section 21(4) 
provides that if the contractor fails to make this payment or any part thereof, the principal employer is liable to 
make this payment and may recover the same from the contractor as set out in that sub-section. Looking to the 
definition of wages Under the said Act read with the definition of wages in the payment of Wages Act, which we 
have set out earlier, it is clear that Section 21 only deals with the payment of contractual wages by the contractor to 
each of his worker; The definition of wages would cover within its scope, inter alia, also those amounts which the 
contractor is liable to pay his workers under any award, settlement or order of court as well as other amounts 
falling within the definition of wages under the payment of Wages Act Subjection (2) provides for a representative 
of the principal employer supervising this payment. Clearly, therefore, the wages which are the subject-matter of 
Section 21 are specified sums which are payable in present by the contractor under the terms of his contract of 
employment with each worker as well as under any existing award, settlement or order of the court. -Section 21 
does not deal with, nor does if cover the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Rules, 1971. Hence Section 
21(4) will not apply to such obligations of the contractor which may be the subject-matter of dispute between the 
contractor and his workers at time of disbursement of wages and which do not fall within the definition of “wages” 
under the Act.” 


(c) Further, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of M/s. Bombay Industries Chemical Industries Vs Deputy 
Labour Commissioner, Civil Appeal Number 813 of 2022, D.O.D dated 4" February 2022, the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court has held that the benefit sought to be enforced under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a pre-existing 
benefit or one flowing from a pre-existing right. The Hon’ble Court added that in the case of Kanku Ben, it is 
observed and held that whenever a workman is entitled to receive from his employer any money or any benefit which 
is capable of being computed in terms of money and which he is entitled to receive from his employer and is denied 
of such benefit can approach Labour Court Under section 33-C(2) of the ID Act. It is further observed that the benefit 
sought to be enforced Under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act is necessarily a preexisting benefit or one flowing from a 
preexisting right. The difference between a preexisting right or benefit on one hand and the right or benefit, which is 
considered just and fair on the other hand is vital. The former falls within jurisdiction of Labour Court exercising 
powers under Section 33C (2) of the ID Act, while the latter does not. 


(d) In the case of Jeet Lal Sharma versus Presiding Officer, 2001 VAD Delhi One, dated 157 March 2000, the 
Hon’ble High Court of Delhi have held:- 


“15. The point which is emphasised is that entitlement to receive money the pre-existing right can the 
based on (1) adjudication (2) settlement (3) service conditions. If the right to get a particular benefit is there, the 
application us. 13-C(2) would be maintainable and jurisdiction of Labour Court will not be barred merely because 
employer has denied the same 


16. What is the meaning of the expression "entitlement in receive". No doubt it is referable to pre-existing 
right. However where the workman claims a benefit flowing from a pre-existing right and approaches the Labour 
Courts 33-612) for computation of the right in term of money and the employer disputes the existences of the right, 
the Labour Court will have the jurisdiction to determine the question, whether the right exists and if the existence 
of right is established than in proceed in compute the benefit flowing therefrom in terms of money or on its 
decisions recovery proceedings start (New Taj Mahal Cafe Private Limited versus Labour Court reported in 1970 
(2) LLN 51 and East India Coal Company Limited (supra) In deciding the maintainability of the application u/s 
13-(12) what is in be looked at is the clans set up in the application and not what the other side contends in its 
reply. The fact that the employer by his plea rises some dispute, does not mean that Jurisdiction of Labour Court to 
deal with the question is taken away.” 


16. Thus, in view of forgone discussion and law laid down by Hon’ble Court as discussed above, Petition filed by the 
Petitioner under Section 33-C(2) of ID Act,1947 against the Respondents for recovery of retrenchment allowances as 
per Ex. W12 is acceptable. Undisputedly, Petitioner was engaged by Respondent No.3 M/s Rishitha Associates, and 
Respondent No.2 has engaged Respondent No. 3 as sub-contractor for Labour supply to work in the establishment of 
Respondent No.1 with prior approval vide document Ex. W8. Therefore, Respondent No.3 as such contractor for

Labour supply for the work is responsible for payment of retrenchment allowances to the Petitioner. It has come on 
record Respondent No.3 has not paid the claimed amount to the Petitioner. Therefore, Respondent No. 3 and 
Respondent No.2 as main contractor is jointly and severally liable for payment of the claimed amount to the 
Petitioner. However, Respondent No.3 has contended that the Petitioner has not been retrenched by him and 
Petitioner is still continuing work with the Respondent No.1 under new contractor. Therefore, Petitioner is not entitled 
to recover retrenchment allowances from Respondent. Undisputedly, Petitioner was engaged by Respondent No.3 to 
work in the establishment of Respondent No.1 for the period from 16.08.2009 to 15.08.2012 as per Ex. W8. 
Respondent No.3 is no more employer of Petitioner after 15.08.2012 of the petitioner w.e.f 16-08-2012 and it makes 
no difference whether petitioner is still working with Respondent No.1 under some other contention. Thus, 
Respondent No.3 has retrenched services of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. 


The definition of retrenchment as provided under Section 2 (00) is extracted as here under: - 


“2(00) “retrenchment “means the termination by the employer f the service of a workman for any reason 
whatsoever, otherwise than as punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action but does not include--- 


(a) Voluntary retirement of the workman: or 


(b) Retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract 
of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a 
stipulation in that behalf; or

contract of employment between the employer and the stipulation in that behalf 
contained therein; or” 


Although Petitioner might be working with Respondent No.1 even after 15.08.2012 but Respondent No.3 is no more 
employer of workman. Therefore, only conclusion can be drawn in such circumstances that Respondent No. 3 has 
terminated the service of Petitioner w.e.f 16.08.2012. Thus, Petitioner is entitled to receive retrenchment/allowance as 
per Ex. W12. Thus, the contention of R3 in this context is untenable. Therefore, the plea of Petitioner that Petitioner 
worker is working now under new contractor is untenable as the Respondent No. 3 is no more employer of the 
Petitioner after 15-08-2012 meaning thereby Petitioner has been terminated by Respondent No. 3 from service 
w.e.f 16.08.2012 and is entitled to receive retrenchment allowances as per terns of the contract. 


17. | However, Respondent No. 1 has contended that terminal benefits claimed by the Petitioner do not form part of 
wages and as such the contractor as direct employer is responsible to make all other payments. In this context, the 
reference of definition of wages u/s 2 ([V) Payment of Wages Act, 1936 is relevant. Therein it is provided that wages 
mean all remuneration (whether by way of salaries, allowances or otherwise) expressed in terms of money are capable 
of being so expressed which would if the terms of employment, expressed or employed were fulfilled be payable to 
person employed in respect of his employer or of work done in such employer and includes. 


(d) Any sum which by reason of termination of employment of the person employed is payable under any law 
contract or instrument which provides for the payment of such sum whether with nor without deduction but does not 
provide for the time within which the payment is to be made. 


Thus, in view of the above definition of wages the retrenchment allowances are very much covered under the 
definition of wages and the contention of the Respondent No.1 that retrenchment allowances are not included under 
the wages is untenable. According to Ex. W12 the term of payment/mode of payment has been agreed upon between 
Respondent No.2 the main contractor and Respondent No.3 sub-contractor, to be paid to the contract Labour 1.6. 
Petitioner for doing the work at Respondent No.1! industry. The employment of Petitioner by Respondent No.3 of the 
Petitioner has been admitted by Respondent No. | & 2 and it is also admitted that retrenchment allowances of the 
Petitioner workman has not been paid by none of the Respondents. Therefore, as a Principal Employer Respondent 
No.1 is liable to pay retrenchment allowance to the Petitioner in view of the provision contained under Section 21 (4) 
of Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 and he may recover the said amount of retrenchment 
allowances so paid to Petitioner from Respondent No. 2 and Respondent No. 3. Thus, the contention of Respondent 
No. 1 in this context is untenable.

1. This is a complaint filed by the complainant u/s 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 raising the 
following contentions: - 


The complainant was appointed by the opposite party in the post of MCS / Office Assistant (Multipurpose) / 
Substaff at their Hunsur branch on 10.12.2004. He submitted application and documents and attended interview for 
selection. Since then he worked continuously in the said branch till the date of his termination / retrenchment / 
discharge / dismissal of his service on 20.10.2016. As a part of his job, he used to open the branch by collecting keys 
from the Manager, cleaning the office, aiding the customers and the branch in various ways. In order to avoid the 
extension of status and benefits of permanent workman to him, the Opposite Party directed the Hunsur branch to debit 
his wages as coolie charges to the General ledger account without obtaining his signature on the debit vouchers. The 
officials of the branch took his signature on the overleaf of coolie paid debit vouchers along with the signatures of the 
branch officers while paying wages in cash to him. He was the only person doing the work of the office attendant / 
messenger / sweeper / substaff / daily wager / MCS etc on coolie charges. The Opposite Party was not marking 
attendance register for his work, not extended payment register to him, signing debit vouchers for his wages by the 
officers of the bank and receiving amount by them and then paying the amounts to him as wages, debiting the wages 
paid to him to General Charges Account instead of salary paid account / Establishment charges, not issuing 
appointment orders or certificates for the services rendered by him in the bank, refusal to pay wages applicable to 
messengers / housekeeping staff / sub staff / MCS to him, not extending the service benefits applicable to permanent 
workman, taking work from him for years together as Coolie by terming his wages as coolie charges practiced by the 
opposite party are all unfair labour practices under the 5" Schedule of the ID Act 1947. The complainant along with 
other coolie workers of the opposite party bank formed a union called Pragathi Grameena Bank Daily Wage Workers 
Union in 2012 and he was active in the Union activities. The Union filed cases before the Central Labour Machinery 
for getting the benefits for the daily wage workers of the Bank. This has caused annoyance to the then management 
against him. CR 15/2015 is pending before this Tribunal in which the Union raised a dispute for regularization of 
services of the workmen including him. He is directly connected with the said dispute and his name appears at 91. No. 
34 in the list of workers. On 20.10.2016, the Branch Manager Mrs. S M Mamatha asked the complainant to work 
under a contractor Gajamukha Agencies in the Bank and on failure his service would be terminated. The complainant 
was not ready to work under a contractor and hence his services are terminated. No other reasons are told by the 
Manager for the termination for his services. Before retrenching his services, the opposite party has not issued any 
notice to him, nor paid any retrenchment compensation, nor paid wages for one month nor conducted any enquiry 
against him. His repeated requests to allow him to do work in the branch were not considered by the Branch Manager. 
The opposite party has not filed any application before the appropriate Government seeking permission to retrench 
him u/s 25 N of the ID Act 1947. Therefore, the retrenchment of his service is illegal, ab-initio void and he is deemed 
to be in the services of the Bank as per sec 25 N(7) of the ID Act. As per the provision of Sec 33 of the ID Act, the 
opposite party cannot alter or change the conditions of his service applicable to him immediately before the 
commencement of the proceedings of C R 15/2015 to his prejudice , during the pendency of CR 15/2015 before this 
Tribunal without the expressed permission in writing from the tribunal and also shall not discharge / dismiss / 
terminate / retrench him unless he was paid wages for one month and without making an application for approval of 
the action so taken. The opposite party has not observed any of the provisions of the ID Act 1947 and has not filed 
any application before the Tribunal. The action of the opposite party is against the provisions of the ID Act, principles 
of natural justice, illegal, null and void. The opposite party was paying him wages @ Rs. 7368/- per month. The 
opposite party has not paid any wages to him since the retrenchment of his services. Since the opposite party has not 
filed any application before the Tribunal seeking approval of their action, he is entitled for payment of full wages 
drawn by him every month till the disposal of this case. Since the opposite party has not filed any application before 
the appropriate government for the termination of his services, not issued any copy of such application to him nor any 
notice / notice pay / compensation as required u/s 25 N of the ID Act, he is deemed to be in service for the benefits as 
applicable to him prior to such cessation of his service and is entitled for wages as per sec 25N (7) of the ID Act. Due 
to the illegal cessation of service imposed on him by the opposite party, the complainant and his family are suffering 
economically and socially. Hence this complaint for declaring the termination / retrenchment / discharge / dismissal 
of the complainant from 20.10.2016 is not in accordance with the provisions of the ID Act 1947, against the principles 
of natural justice, arbitrary, unilateral, ill motivated and illegal and to direct the opposite party to reinstate the 
complainant with full back wages, continuity of service with regularization, ancillary benefits from 20.10.2016 and 
with cost. 


2 The opposite party at the outset has contended that the complainant has no enforceable cause of action to 
raise Industrial Dispute and has no right to seek employment in the bank and there is no discharge or termination of 
employment and hence no Industrial Dispute lie under Industrial Disputes Act 1947. It is equally contended that there 
is no post of messenger cum sweeper in the bank. The opposite party inter alia contended that based on the man 
power requirement assessed by the bank as per the guidelines issued by the Government of India at the end of March 
every year, the total vacancies to be filled up by the direct recruitment and promotions will be identified and the 
process of direct recruitment and promotions will be initiated after obtaining permissions from the Sponsor Bank viz., 
Canara Bank and the Board of the opposite party bank. Recruitment and appointment of employees in the Regional 
Rural Banks is governed by the rules framed by the Government of India vide notification dated 13.07.2010 called 


536 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 24, 2026/MAGHA 4, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


“Regional Rural Banks (Appointment and Promotions of Officers and Employees) Rules 2010”. As per the said rules, 
procedure with regard to Office Attendant (Multipurpose Group C employees) are prescribed, the selection process 
being on the basis of interview to be conducted by a Committee. The branches / offices of the bank engage coolies 
occasionally and intermittently as and when necessitated for doing menial works in the branches. In order to meet the 
exigencies of the work, the opposite party bank branches used to engage coolies only for few hours for such menial 
works like cleaning, sweeping and watering and were paid coolie charges proportionately depending upon the number 
of hours they worked. The complainant was also engaged similarly as a coolie intermittently and not continuously. 
Depending upon the availability of the person in the locale, the Branch Manager engaged such person on need basis 
for such works. As per the Government of India guidelines for appointment of Regular Attendants, the names should 
be sponsored by the employment exchange and such engagement is also subject to the conditions stipulated in regard 
to educational qualification, age etc. While engaging the coolies, no educational qualifications or age were looked into 
and whoever is available would be engaged. The persons so engaged are at liberty to work elsewhere after completion 
of the menial works entrusted to them. They are not governed by any rules and regulation of the bank and there is no 
employee employer relationship as they have not been engaged by the bank against the post. It is the settled position 
in law that a person engaged intermittently on daily wages will not have the right to be absorbed for any post. The 
Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi held that there is no right to those who have 
been engaged as daily wagers temporarily or on contractual basis to claim that they have the right to be absorbed in 
service as they cannot be said to be holders of post. In Union of India vs. A $ Pillai also the Hon'ble Supreme Court 
held that daily wager / part time workers not engaged in any regular cadres or any sanctioned post are not entitled for 
absorption. The contention of the complainant that he was appointed by the opposite party at their Hunsur branch on 
10.12.2004 by taking application form etc. is denied. The Branch Manager has no power to recruit / appoint any 
employee. The complainant was engaged only occasionally to attend to menial / urgent works and not continuously. 
Since the complainant was not recruited / appointed by the opposite party anytime, his termination / dismissal / 
retrenchment on 20.10.2016 did not arise. Consequently, question of issuing notice to him, payment of retrenchment 
compensation, payment of wages of one month, filing of application before the Tribunal before or during the 
pendency of CR 15/2015 and seeking permission u/s 25N of the Act does not arise. Under the circumstances, sec 33 
of the Industrial Disputes Act has no application in his case. He was never engaged for attending the regular functions 
of substaff. He was paid wages for the occasional / casual works he was engaged to. The Branch Managers are not 
authorized to issue any certificates and question of issuing certificates to him does not arise as he was not 
continuously engaged in the opposite party bank and nor was empanelled in the daily wagers’ list. The complainant 
has not been appointed in the payrolls of the opposite party at any time. Since he has not been appointed in the 
opposite party bank, question of marking in the attendance register, extending payment registered to him, debiting the 
payment made to him to salary account, issuing appointment orders, issuing certificates and denying benefits etc. did 
not arise. Hence the allegation of unfair labour practice on the part of the II Party is untenable. The contention of the 
complainant that his involvement in the union activities and filing of Industrial Dispute by the said union for getting 
benefits to the daily wage workers has caused anger to the opposite party is a figment of his imagination and hence 
denied. The complainant was not working in the opposite party bank on continuous basis and was engaged 
occasionally, casually for menial and urgent requirements. His contention that he was being paid wages @ Rs. 7368/- 
is denied. His contentions that he was deemed to be in service and entitled for benefits are untenable and baseless. 
The complainant has not undergone any process of recruitment and is not entitled for recruitment for appointment in 
the opposite party bank or for reinstatement or other ancillary benefits as claimed by him. For all these reasons, the 
opposite party has prayed for rejection of the complaint. 


3. From the above rival pleadings, following points arise for consideration:- 

1. Whether the complaint is legally and factually maintainable? 

2. Whether the Complainant is proved to have been working continuously in the opposite party establishment 
since 10.12.2004? 

3. Whether the complainant is proved to have been discharged / terminated / retrenched / dismissed from 
service as contended by him? 

4. Whether the alleged contravention of the provision of sec 33 of the ID Act is proved by the complainant? 

5. Whether the complainant is entitled to get reinstatement to the service with full back wages, continuity of 
service and ancillary benefits from 20.10.2016 as prayed for? 

6. What is the proper Order and Award to be passed in this complaint case? 

4. Either of the parties did not prefer to adduce any evidence in the matter. Though the complainant is seen to 


have filed an affidavit dated 07.01.2021 in lieu of his examination in chief and sought time for further examination in 
chief, he did not thenceforth prefer to make him available for further examination in chief or cross-examination. 


5. Heard the oral and written arguments submitted from both sides. 


6. Points no. 1 to 4:- Since all these points are closely integrated and inter-twined, all these points are 
discussed together. Alleging contravention of the provisions of sec 33 of the ID Act 1947, the complainant filed the 
instant complaint u/s 33A of the Act on the factual averment that the opposite party has not filed any application 


[भाग --खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 537 


before this Tribunal seeking permission for retrenching / terminating / dismissing him on 20.10.2016 and not filing 
any application for approval of their said action. The complainant’s case is that he was appointed by the opposite 
party bank at their Hunsur branch on 10.12.2004 on submission of application and subjecting him for interview and 
on obtaining documents from him. He claims that since then he has worked continuously in the said branch on all 
working days. It is his further case that on 20.10.2014, the then Branch Manager asked him to work under a contractor 
Gajamukha Agencies and in the event he does not heed to that, not to come for work anymore and eventually he 
services are terminated by the opposite party as he was not ready to work under a contractor. This particular averment, 
the opposite party emphatically disputed. The complainant inter alia pleaded that he is an active member in a Union 
under the name and style Pragathi Grameena Bank Daily Wage Workers Union formed between himself with other 
coolie workers of the opposite party bank. The said union has raised a dispute for regularization of the service of the 
complainant and other similarly placed coolie before the Central Government Machinery and the same is registered 
and pending before this Tribunal as CR 15/2015. It is the case of the complainant that he is directly connected with 
the said dispute raised by the Union pending before this Tribunal. The disengagement of job on 20.10.2016 according 
to the complainant tantamounts to contravention of the provisions of sec 33 of the ID Act as according to him, it 
happened when the industrial dispute raised by the union for and on behalf of him and the other coolie workers was 
pending adjudication. This gave way for filing this complaint u/s 33A of the ID Act. 


7. Oral and written arguments are advanced on behalf of the complainant narrating all these events by his 
authorized representative. 


8. The learned counsel for the opposite party per contra put forth his rival submission that the complainant has 
never ever rendered any continuous service in the opposite party bank. Instead the bank was in the practice of 
engaging persons from the locale for attending menial job like sweeping, cleaning and watering whenever so 
necessitated and such persons were paid coolie charges for the same. According to the opposite party, the complainant 
was also so casually engaged occasionally and intermittently depending on the requirement of the branch as a coolie 
for doing menial works and such works carried out by him was not regular in nature, but only on need basis. 


9. Of course, the event of non-engagement for work said to have happened on 20.10.2016 is apparently during 
the pendency of CR 15/2015. However the complainant did not prefer to bring home any proof that he was in service 
in the opposite party bank even on the previous day or anytime there-before in a constant and continuous stretch so as 
to establish the retrenchment / dismissal / discharge / termination alleged in the complaint. Here it is contextually 
profitable to quote Sec 33 of the Act:- 


33. [ Conditions of service, etc., to remain unchanged under certain circumstances during pendency of 
proceedings. ] 


(1)During the pendency of any conciliation proceeding before a conciliation officer or a Board or of any 
proceeding before ][an arbitrator or] [a Labour Court or Tribunal or National Tribunal in respect of an 
industrial dispute, no employer shall- (a)in regard to any matter connected with the dispute, alter, to the 
prejudice of the workmen concerned in such dispute, the conditions of service applicable to them immediately 
before the commencement of such proceeding; or (b)for any misconduct connected with the dispute, discharge 
or punish, whether by dismissal or otherwise, any workmen concerned in such dispute, ave with the express 
permission in writing of the authority before which the proceeding is pending.(2)During the pendency of any 
such proceeding in respect of an industrial dispute, the employer may, in accordance with the standing orders 
applicable to a workman concerned in such dispute ] [or, where there are no such standing orders, in 
accordance with the terms of the contract, whether express or implied, between him and the workman] (a)[ 
alter, in regard to any matter not connected with the dispute, the conditions of service applicable to that 
workman immediately before the commencement of such proceeding; or (b) for any misconduct not connected 
with the dispute, discharge or punish, whether by dismissal or otherwise, that workman: Provided that no such 
workman shall be discharged or dismissed, unless he has been paid wages for one month and an application 
has been made by the employer to the authority before which the proceeding is pending for approval of the 
action taken by the employer. (3)Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (2), no employer shall, 
during the pendency of any such proceeding in respect of an industrial dispute, take any action against any 
protected workman concerned in such dispute (a) by altering, to the prejudice of such protected workman, the 
conditions of service applicable to him immediately before the commencement of such proceedings; or (b) by 
discharging or punishing, whether by dismissal or otherwise, such protected workman, save with the express 
permission in writing of the authority before which the proceeding is pending. Explanation:-For the purposes of 
this sub-section, a "protected workman ", in relation to an establishment, means a workman who, being] [a 
member of the executive or other office bearer] [of a registered trade union connected with the establishment, is 
recognised as such in accordance with rules made in this behalf.(4)In every establishment, the number of 
workmen to be recognised as protected workmen for the purposes of sub-section (3) shall be one per cent. of the 
total number of workmen employed therein subject to a minimum number of five protected workmen and a 
maximum number of one hundred protected workmen and for the aforesaid purpose, the appropriate 
Government may make rules providing for the distribution of such protected workmen among various trade 
unions, if any, connected with the establishment and the manner in which the workmen may be chosen and
